Download and Installation of the VG_GNU_PACKAGE
Several GNU GCC compiler versions are provided in the VG_GNU_PACKAGE along
with GNU tools (linker, assembler, and so on). Use the VG_GNU_PACKAGE for SystemC
compilation.

Download and Installation of the VG_GNU_PACKAGE
Installing and Using GCC 13.3.0
Use one of the following methods to install GCC 13.3.0:
• Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Outside a VCS Image
• Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Without Sourcing the source_me File
• Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Inside a VCS Image
The Linux host must have a 64-bit OS and CPU.
Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Outside a VCS Image
Follow the instructions provided in this section in either of the following scenarios:
• Installing the VG_GNU_PACKAGE outside the VCS image.
• Using the package for all VCS applications but not for SystemC.
You must add both gcc and binutils to the path. To update your path, use the
source_me scripts.
To install the default GCC version, perform the following steps:
1. Set up your environment by using the following commands:
% mkdir -p <path_to_vg_gnu_directory>/gnu
% cd <path_to_vg_gnu_directory>/gnu
2. Download the tar.gz file from the FTP server.
3. Untar the package.
4. Set the following VG_GNU_PACKAGE environment variable:
Bash (sh) users must execute the following commands:
% export VG_GNU_PACKAGE=<path_to_vg_gnu_directory>/gnu/linux
% $VG_GNU_PACKAGE/source_me.sh
C Shell (csh or tcsh) users must execute the following commands:
% setenv VG_GNU_PACKAGE
<path_to_vg_gnu_directory>/gnu/linux
% source $VG_GNU_PACKAGE/source_me.csh
When you source the source_me setup script from the VG_GNU_PACKAGE, the path to the
GCC shared libraries is prefixed with the LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

Download and Installation of the VG_GNU_PACKAGE
Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Without Sourcing the
source_me File
This setup applies to Linux32 and Linux64 only.
If you cannot source one of the source_me files, use the xbin directory as an alternative.
Refer to Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Outside a VCS Image to download and
install the VG_GNU_PACKAGE. However, do not source the VG GNU source_me file. Instead,
use gcc in the xbin directory. For example,
% <path_to_vg_gnu_directory>/gnu/linux/gcc/xbin/gcc myfile.c
In this case, xbin is used, not the bin. When you call the compiler through the xbin
directory, it automatically selects the corresponding binutils (assembler and linker). You
cannot override the location of binutils.
Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Inside a VCS Image
The easiest method to use the VG_GNU_PACKAGE for VCS simulations that contain
SystemC is to install the package inside a VCS image. After installation, VCS
automatically uses this package for the VCS SystemC flow (for example, when you use
the syscan command).
Install the image at $VCS_HOME/gnu. The directory structure must be as shown in the
following figure:
Figure 3 VCS_HOME/gnu Directory Structure
$VCS_HOME/gnu/
linux/
g cc
b inutils
1. Download the linux_gcc1330_default.tar.gz package for your platform by using
the instructions provided in the Installing and Setting Up GCC 13.3.0 Outside a VCS
Image section.
2. Set up your environment by using the following commands:
% setenv VCS_HOME <VCS_installation_directory>
% cd $VCS_HOME

% mkdir gnu
% cd gnu
3. Untar the package by using the following command:
% gtar -zxvf linux_gcc1330_default.tar.gz
Do not set the VG_GNU_PACKAGE environment variable or source any setup script. When
VG_GNU_PACKAGE is set up in this manner, VCS automatically uses $VCS_HOME/gnu for the
VCS SystemC flow.
However, setting the VG_GNU_PACKAGE environment variable to a value disables the
automatic selection of GCC from $VCS_HOME/gnu. Therefore, before you use this feature,
unset the environment variable, as follows:
% unsetenv VG_GNU_PACKAGE
You can override the default with explicit command-line arguments such as -cc, -cpp, or
ld. Command-line arguments always take precedence over the default GNU package. It is
the only method to override the default compiler version.
VCS does not use the VG_GNU_PACKAGE when you are outside the VCS SystemC flow. For
example, calling % vcs top.v without the -sysc argument does not automatically infer
VG_GNU_PACKAGE. Instead, VCS uses the compiler in the current path as usual.
Prefixing the Path to Shared GCC Libraries With
LD_LIBRARY_PATH
As part of sourcing the setup script (by using source) from the VG_GNU_PACKAGE, the
path to the shared libraries of the GCC installation is prefixed with the LD_LIBRARY_PATH
variable. This ensures that the compiler and libraries are in synchronization with each
other.
Appending the path to the location of the libraries with the LD_LIBRARY_PATH can cause
issues.

Firefox, Chrome, and Safari are the recommended browsers for SolvNetPlus. It

Maximum Number of Command-Line Characters
There is a known limit to the number of characters that can appear on a vhdlan, vlogan,
or vcs command-line. This limit varies from platform to platform, but all platforms have
a limit. You can work around this limitation by using these commands with the -f or -F
options. These options specify a file that can contain compile-time options and source file
names.

Chapter 13: Limitations and Known Issues
Limitations
Limitations on Coverage Metrics
The following are the limitations on coverage metrics:
• VCS does not monitor the following language constructs in the IEEE Std 1364-1995
and 1364-2001 for condition or FSM coverage.
◦ Memories in Condition Coverage
VCS does not monitor condition coverage sub-expressions that contain memory
elements. VCS also does not extract FSMs where the current and next state of the
FSM are in memory elements.
◦ Multidimensional Arrays in FSM Coverage
VCS does not monitor condition coverage or extract FSM coverage for
multidimensional array elements.
Word Flow Support of the Verification Planner Doc Annotator
The Verification Planner Word Doc Annotator does not support OpenOffice XML input.
Only MS Word 2003 or newer versions are supported. This limitation applies only to the
Word flow. The spreadsheet flow supports both MS Excel and OpenOffice.
Limitations on VHDL 2008 Support
The following features are not supported on VHDL 2008 support:
• Enhanced generic-mapped packages
• The VHDL 2008 Local Packages feature is not supported for Coverage, Debug, Xprop,
NLP, and Verdi.
• The Unconstrained Elements in Generics and Generic Types feature has the following
limitations:
◦ The port associations at the VHDL/Verilog boundary is not supported.
◦ The type conversions are not supported.
◦ This feature is not supported for Coverage, Debug, Xprop, NLP, and Verdi.
• The VHDL Unconstrained Generic Formal Sub Element Association (FSA) feature is
not supported for multidimensional arrays FSA.
• The VHDL 2008 Generics in Subprograms feature is not supported in the KDB,
Coverage, and Xprop flows.

Limitations
• The VHDL 2008 Record Type Conversions feature has the following limitations:
◦ The partially constrained array subtypes are not supported.
◦ Type conversions to a record subtype with unconstrained elements are not
supported.
Limitations on a VHDL Top Design
The following are the limitations on a VHDL top design:
• Only line, condition, and toggle coverage are available for the VHDL part of a mixed-
language design.
• ovaan -f file : The -f switch to ovaan is currently not supported.
• The -ova_debug and -ova_debug_vpd options are currently not supported. (Viewing of
assertion results with Verdi is also not supported.)
• The unit versions of the OVA Checker Library standard checkers are currently not
supported. Use only the template versions.
• The following items are not supported in inlined OVA:
◦ Memory in binding. For example,
bind module M : U I (clk, mem[addr]);
Here, mem is a declared multidimensional (two or more) array — for example, reg
[7:0] mem [255:0];
◦ VHDL extended identifiers in the design
◦ Assertions bound to instances inside a generate hierarchy
• OpenVera Assertions in the VHDL part of a mixed-signal design require the SUN
Solaris 9 (5.9 2.9) platform.
• Attributes like 'delayed(20 ns ) are not locally static, and so they are not allowed in
port bindings. They are not allowed in ordinary binding indications (pre-incremental
binding) so they are not supported yet with incremental binding either.
• In the C Language Interface (VHPI), there is a limitation on iteration over all callbacks
on Linux platforms.
Iterators created to get all the callbacks registered in a simulation run do not scan
through the value change callbacks for objects on the event side.

Checkpoint and Rewind
Checkpoint and rewind has not been tested with any of the third-party tool.
Methodology for Save and Restore
The following use models are supported for saving and restoring a simulation:
• Save using UCLI commands and restore using UCLI commands.
• Save the simulation state in Verdi and restore the state in Verdi.
• Save the simulation state in UCLI and restore the state in Verdi.
The following use model is not supported for saving and restoring a simulation:
• Save the simulation state in Verdi and restore the state using UCLI commands

Chapter 13: Limitations and Known Issues
Known Issues
You must close all external applications that communicate with VCS using the VHPI or
PLI, before you save and restore a simulation.
For more information on save and restore, see the Saving and Restarting the Simulation
section in the VCS User Guide, and the Restrictions for Save and Restore Commands
section in the Unified Command Line Interface User Guide.
Using an External Memory Manager
The internal memory manager in VCS relies on the following documented feature of
malloc:
void *malloc(size_t size);
The malloc() and free() functions provide a simple general-purpose memory allocation
package. The malloc() function returns a pointer to a block of at least size bytes suitably
aligned for any use.
Certain restrictive memory managers may choose to enforce a fixed memory alignment.
This can lead to unaligned accesses in some situations, which may produce bus errors.
If you want to use an external memory manager, Synopsys recommends thoroughly
reviewing the memory manager’s documentation for issues related to the alignment of
memory returned.
Displaying Value of Loop Variable in Verdi and UCLI
SystemVerilog enables you to declare the for loop control variable within a for loop. This
creates a local variable within the loop. In some cases, Verdi and UCLI cannot display the
value of a control variable declared within a for loop statement. The value can be printed
using the $display system task. The workaround is to move the declaration of the control
variable outside the for loop.
For example,
initial begin
for (int j=0;j<5;j++) begin
$display("j=%0d\n",j);
end
end
Workaround:
initial begin
int j;

P2P Glitch Corruption Persists When Destination Value Remains
Unchanged After Fan-in Toggle
P2P glitch corruption on a destination might not be cleared by a design-driven update on
its fan-in if the recomputed value for the destination remains unchanged (for example,
AND/OR short-circuit). The corruption persists until the glxdelta timeout, instead of being
cleared at the update time.

Overview
This document discusses two analysis techniques – merging and grading – that are used
to analyze the results of coverage-enabled regression runs. Merging combines data from
multiple tests and VDBs to produce a single unified VDB that contains the combined
results of all your test runs. Once the data is merged, you can generate reports or load
the merged data into Verdi to analyze the results. On the other hand, grading means
comparing the effectiveness of tests for coverage. Grading is useful when you want to
eliminate redundant tests from a test suite, arrange tests in a best-first order, or analyze
how much new coverage is added by a new regression run.
This document consists of the following sections:
• Merging
• Grading

Merging
For many designs, multiple simulations are required to close on all coverage areas. These
simulations yield coverage databases that represent different flows through the design.
After executing multiple simulations, you can merge the coverage databases that they
produced to get a single merged VDB containing all their combined results.
URG provides two methods of merging – serial and parallel merging. URG uses serial
merging as the default mechanism to merge test results. As the name implies, this
technique merges the coverage data of tests one after the other, serially. Coverage data
can be merged in parallel by specifying the -parallel option on the URG command line
to significantly speed up processing. You can direct URG to do the merging in parallel,
either on a single machine, on multiple machines, or on a compute farm/grid.
This section consists of the following subsections:
• Managing Coverage Data Files
• Merge Techniques
Managing Coverage Data Files
Using coverage produces some additional files and directories at compile and simulation
time. This section discusses how to manage the creation of these files, and how to merge
coverage data from multiple simulations.
When you compile with VCS, the executable name determines the name of the database
created. For example, the following command creates a binary executable simv1 and
a corresponding simv1.vdb directory, which contains compile-time coverage-related
information:
vcs -o simv1 file1.v file2.v -cm line+tgl
This section consists of the following subsections:
• Redirecting Coverage Data to the Directory of Your Choice
• Generating a Merged Database

Managing Coverage Data Files
Redirecting Coverage Data to the Directory of Your Choice
To redirect coverage data to the directory of your choice, use the -cm_dir option in the
following ways:
1. Use the -cm_dir Option With Compile and Run Commands
The -cm_dir option is used to dump coverage data of multiple regressions to
a merged directory. For example, to dump compile-time data (design data) to
regress1_design.vdb use the following command:
vcs -cm line+tgl file5.v -cm_dir regress1_design.vdb
You can dump each simulation data (test data) to different directories. For example,
to dump test1 to regress1_run1.vdb and test2 to regress1_run2.vdb, use the
following commands:
simv -cm line+tgl -cm_dir regress1_run1.vdb -cm_name test1
-cm_test /regr1/run1/test1
simv -cm line+tgl -cm_dir regress1_run2.vdb -cm_name test2
-cm_test /regr1/run1/test2
In the example, the -cm_test option is used in conjunction with the -cm_name option
to specify the name of the test on the simv command line. The -cm_name option
designates a unique test name under the directory (created using the -cm_dir option).
The -cm_test option assigns the test an unambiguous name.
2. Use of -cm_dir at Compile Time Only
You can dump all simulation coverage data to the VDB directory specified at compile
time. For example, to dump both design data and test data to the regress2.vdb
directory specified at the compile time, use the following command:
vcs -cm line+tgl+fsm file3.v file4.v -cm_dir regress2.vdb

Generating a Merged Database
To merge all the coverage data collected from multiple regressions, use the -dbname
option on the URG command line. If both design and test data for all simulation runs are in
the same directory regress2.vdb, use the following command to produce a merged VDB
named mymerge.vdb:
urg -dir regress2.vdb -dbname mymerge.vdb

Chapter 2: Merging
Merge Techniques
You can merge multiple VDB directories by specifying them after the -dir option on the
URG command line. The input VDBs can be generated at compile time, at simulation time,
or by another merge operation. For example:
urg -dir regress2_design.vdb regress2_run1.vdb mymerge.vdb -dbname
simv2.vdb ----_-noreport
This command reads all the specified VDB directories and merges them to create a new
VDB directory named simv2.vdb. The -noreport option does not generate a report at the
same time. It is better to generate reports separately.
If you have a long list of VDB directories to be merged, you can use the -f option to URG.
This option enables you to specify all the databases for merging in a file. For example, the
following urg -f command takes the list of databases for merging from the vdblist file:
urg -f vdblist -dbname final_merge.vdb -noreport
Merge Techniques
This section explains different merging techniques for the following metrics:
• Functional Coverage
• Code Coverage
Functional Coverage
Functional coverage consists of two metric types: covergroups and cover properties/
assertions.
This section focuses on providing information on covergroup merging and consists of the
following subsections:
• Basic Options and Switches for Covergroup Merging
• Covergroup Shapes in a Design
• Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Basic Options and Switches for Covergroup Merging
If a module contains a covergroup instance, then each instance of the module has a
separate covergroup reported for it. For example, consider the following mymod module:
module mymod;
…
mygroup g1 = new(x, y, z);
endmodule

Merge Techniques
If there are the following three instances of mymod, they would each be reported
separately:
top.inst1::addum
top.inst2::addum
top.inst3::addum
This separation ensures that just because a bin is covered in one instance, it does not
appear that the same testing has been done in the other instances.
To override this creation of multiple groups, use the -group merge_across_scopes on
the URG command line. This is useful when the goal of the group is explicitly to span the
behavior across all instances instead of tracking coverage separately for each instance of
the module.
If a module contains multiple covergroup instances, then the computation of the module's
coverage score depends on each instance's coverage score. For example, consider the
following mymod1 module with covergroup instances g1 and g2:
module mymod1;
…
mygroup g1 = new(x, y, z);
mygroup g2 = new(p, q, r);
endmodule
To track the coverage information for a covergroup instance, check its per_instance
option. If option.per_instance = 1 , the coverage information for the covergroup
instance is tracked. By default, its value is false, that is, option.per_instance=0.
Covergroup Shapes in a Design
Merging of a covergroup is determined by its shape as explained below:
• If the shapes of two covergroups are same, then the coverage data for two coverage
models is mergeable.
• If the shapes of two covergroups are different, then the coverage data for two coverage
models becomes non-mergable. In this case, based on the merge options specified on
the URG command line, it is decided which shape should be retained or discarded in
the final merged database.
Covergroup instances are also reported separately when their shapes are different. The
shape of a covergroup is determined by the covergroup parameters and the bins in each
coverpoint and cross in the group. Therefore, if a covergroup is passed a 16-bit argument
in one case, and a 32-bit argument in another, VCS splits it into two different shapes
that are reported separately, even if they are instantiated in the same scope. When a
covergroup is split into shapes this way, VCS uses the base name of the group and adds

the parameter values that differentiate the shapes. For example, if a parameter p is used
to determine the number of bins in a coverpoint, the report is as follows:
top.inst1::addum::SHAPE{p=16}
top.inst1::addum::SHAPE{p=32}
There is no way to override this, as the different shapes cannot be merged in a meaningful
way.
Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Covergroup shape can change due to the changes in the covergroup definition itself. For
example, Day1 version of a group may have 16 bins for one of its coverpoints, but Day2
could have 32 bins for that coverpoint.

• Union Merging

Union Merging
Union merging allows you to merge the data from the latest versions of your covergroup
models with the data collected from previous versions. This flow allows you to merge
the data and retain single covergroups from different versions. Therefore, the merged
database contains multiple versions of coverpoints inside a given group.
To perform union merging of covergroups, use the -flex_merge union switch as follows:
urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb … simvN.vdb -flex_merge union -dbname
merged.vdb -noreport

To perform union merging of covergroups, use the -flex_merge union switch as follows:
urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb … simvN.vdb -flex_merge union -dbname
merged.vdb -noreport
Reference Merging
Reference merging allows you to choose a reference design from the VDB directories
that are created with union merging, and may thus contain multiple versions of different
covergroups. Reference merging enables you to produce a report from a single version of
your design. To perform reference merging, use the -flex_merge reference switch as
follows:
urg -dir final_day.vdb merged.vdb -flex_merge reference
The switch considers only the coverage data that matches the reference version. If your
reference version has an 8-bit coverpoint in the top.d1::g group, then only the data from
the 8-bit versions of that coverpoint are merged in the final report.
You should decide which merging strategy you should use early in the cycle and run test
merges to make sure it satisfies your requirements.

Code Coverage
Mapping is what URG calls for merging the coverage results from different subsets of the
input designs.
A common use of mapping is to merge the coverage results collected for a sub-block onto
the SOC coverage model of the full design. For example, the coverage for the md3 block in
the figure below is merged onto all instances of its top module in the base design using the
-map option on the URG command line:
When mapping, the coverage of any unmapped modules, such as tbblk in this example,
is ignored. This allows you to peel off the testbench from a block and just copy the design
coverage. The default option is simple and module-based. To perform more sophisticated
mapping on an instance-by-instance basis, -map use the -mapfile option.

Grading
Grading, or test ranking, means comparing the effectiveness of tests for coverage.
Grading is useful when you want to eliminate redundant tests from a test suite, arrange
tests in a best-first order, or compare the coverage effectiveness of a new regression run
to coverage collected in a previously-merged VDB directory.
Grading can select tests based purely on coverage score, minimizing the total number of
tests required to hit the coverage score hit by the whole database, or it can be directed
to select tests to minimize total CPU time, simulation cycles, or wall clock time. The basic
grading command is as follows:
urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -parallel -grade
If you add the -show tests switch to the URG command line when created a merged
VDB directory, you can grade directly from the merged VDB. This allows you to
consolidate all coverage information in a single VDB so that individual simulation VDB
directories do not have to be retained. For example, to create a merged VDB suitable for
grading, use the following command:
urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -dbname merged.vdb -noreport -show tests
You can then grade directly from this VDB using the following command:
urg -dir merged.vdb -grade
Some useful options for grading are given in the table below. Provide these options
anywhere after the -grade option on the URG command line:
Options Description
indexlimit N Retains at most N tests per covered object. Higher N uses more
memory and time but produces more precise grading results.
testfile Generates a file, gradedtests.txt, in the urgReport directory that is a
simple ordered list of the graded tests.

Overview
Merging combines data from multiple tests and databases to produce a unified database
that contains the combined results of all your tests. Once the data is merged, you can
generate reports or load the merged data into Verdi or URG to analyze the results. For
many designs, multiple simulations are required to close on all coverage areas. These
simulations yield coverage databases that represent different flows through the designs.
After executing multiple simulations, you can merge these coverage databases to get a
single-merged database containing all the combined results.
Merging coverage from multiple tests in a database results in a logical OR of the coverage
status of the merged objects. If a coverage object is covered in any test, then the object is
covered in the merged database. For example, consider that simulations are run for test1
and test2 of the simv database as follows:
simv <coverage_options> -cm_test /simv/test1
simv <coverage_options> -cm_test /simv/test2
If test1 covers obj1 and test2 covers obj2, the merged database of these two tests
covers both obj1 and obj2.
This document covers the following topics:
• Code Coverage Merging
• Functional Coverage Merging

Code Coverage Merging
While merging code coverage across multiple databases, the objects and instances in the
base database are used as a reference. The base database is the most recent version
of the design and the input database is another database to be merged with the base
database. If there are multiple input databases, each database is merged one at a time
with the base database.
Consider that simulations are run for base.vdb and input.vdb, and their simv commands
are as follows:
simv <coverage options> -cm_dir base.vdb
simv <coverage options> -cm_dir input.vdb
To merge the base and input databases, use the following command:
urg -dir base.vdb input.vdb -dbname merged
This command reads base.vdb and input.vdb, and merges them to create a new
database named merged.vdb.
If two databases are compiled with the same options and versions of the design, the
coverage status of each object in each module and instance is merged. For example, if
the m11.inst11 instance in the base database, base.vdb, covers the sig1 signal and
the input database, input.vdb, covers the sig2 signal in that instance, the merged result
covers both sig1 and sig2.
The following table shows the data covered in the merged database if both databases are
generated with the same options and versions of the design:
Object In Base In Input In Merged
obj1 Covered Covered Covered
obj2 Covered Covered Covered
obj3 Not covered Covered Covered
obj4 Covered Not covered Covered

Chapter 2: Code Coverage Merging
Module-Based Mapping
If there are differences between the two designs, by default the base design's data is
used and the input design's data is not used, on a module-by-module and instance-by-
instance basis. For example, if there is a signal sig3 in the input design in the m11.inst11
instance that does not exist in the base design, all the input design's toggle coverage
for that instance is ignored, and only the signals covered in the base design's tests are
reported as covered in the merged result.
If the design hierarchy is different in the databases that you are trying to merge, coverage
in mismatched parts of the design are not merged. For example, consider the following
figure in which the m11 module in input.vdb cannot be directly merged with the
m11 module in base.vdb as they belong to different hierarchies, that is tb1 and m1,
respectively:
To merge coverage data from non-identical design hierarchies, use mapping. A common
usage is to merge the coverage results collected from a sub-block onto the SoC coverage
model of the full design. For example, to merge the coverage for m11 in input.vdb in the
above figure onto all instances of its top module, m1, in base.vdb, use the -map option.
The default -map option is simple and used for module-based mapping. To perform more

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
full design. For example, to merge the coverage for m11 in input.vdb in the
above figure onto all instances of its top module, m1, in base.vdb, use the -map option.
The default -map option is simple and used for module-based mapping. To perform more
sophisticated mapping on an instance-by-instance basis, use the -mapfile option.
For more details on module-based mapping and instance-based mapping, see the
following sections:
• Module-Based Mapping
• Instance-Based Mapping
Module-Based Mapping
Module-based mapping allows you to view the combined coverage for the module's
instantiations in two different hierarchies. To perform module-based mapping, use the

Chapter 2: Code Coverage Merging
Instance-Based Mapping
-map option. For example, the following command merges the coverage data for the m11
module from base.vdb and input.vdb (see the above figure):
urg -dir base.vdb input.vdb -map m11
For more details on module-based mapping, see the "Mapping Coverage Metrics" section
in Chapter 5, "Merging Coverage Metrics" of the Coverage Technology User Guide.
Instance-Based Mapping
Instance-based mapping allows you to specify an instance in your base database in
which you want to merge coverage data of two different databases. In the example, you
can merge instances namely input.tb1.m11.inst11 and input.tb2.m2.inst2 to the
base.m1.m11.inst11 instance. The mapping configuration file for this example contains
the following information:
MODULE: m11
INSTANCE:
SRC: input.tb1.m11.inst11, input.tb2.m2.inst2
DST: base.m1.m11.inst11
To perform instance-based mapping, use the -mapfile option as follows:
urg -dir base.vdb input.vdb -mapfile <mapping_config_file>
For more details on instance-based mapping, see the "Understanding Instance-Based
Mapping" section in Chapter 5, "Merging Coverage Metrics" of the Coverage Technology
User Guide.

Functional Coverage Merging
Merging functional coverage is same as merging code coverage except it is valid to merge
the parts of the coverage model that are identical when the functional coverage model
changes over time. For example, if 0.01% of the functional coverage model changes
between databases, it is valid to merge the remaining 99.99%. The same is not true for
code coverage because a small change in a module’s implementation can invalidate
merging the module.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Covergroup Shapes in a Design
• Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Covergroup Shapes in a Design
Merging of a covergroup is determined by its shape as explained below:
• If the shapes of two covergroups are same, then the coverage data for two coverage
models is mergeable.
• If the shapes of two covergroups are different, then the coverage data for two coverage
models becomes non-mergeable. In this case, based on the merge options specified
on the URG command line, it is decided which shape should be retained or discarded
in the final merged database.
Covergroup instances are also reported separately when their shapes are different. The
shape of a covergroup is determined by the covergroup parameters and the bins in each
coverpoint and cross in the group. Therefore, if a covergroup is passed a 16-bit argument
in one case, and a 32-bit argument in another, VCS splits it into two different shapes
that are reported separately, even if they are instantiated in the same scope. When a
covergroup is split into shapes this way, VCS uses the base name of the group and adds
the parameter values that differentiate the shapes. For example, if a parameter p is used
to determine the number of bins in a coverpoint, the report is as follows:
m11.inst11::addum::SHAPE{p=16}
m11.inst11::addum::SHAPE{p=32}

Chapter 3: Functional Coverage Merging
Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
There is no way to override this, as the different shapes cannot be merged in a meaningful
way.
Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Covergroup shape can change due to the changes in the covergroup definition itself. For
example, Day1 version of a group may have 16 bins for one of its coverpoints, but Day2
could have 32 bins for that coverpoint.
This section consists of the following topics:
• Union Merging
• Reference Merging
Union Merging
Union merging allows you to merge the data from the latest versions of your covergroup
models with the data collected from previous versions. This flow allows you to merge
the data and retain single covergroups from different versions. Therefore, the merged
database may contain multiple versions of coverpoints inside a given group.
To perform union merging of covergroups, use the -flex_merge union switch as follows:
urg -dir day1.vdb day2.vdb … dayN.vdb -flex_merge union -dbname
merged.vdb
Reference Merging
Reference merging allows you to choose a reference design from the databases that
are created with union merging, and may thus contain multiple versions of different
covergroups. Reference merging enables you to produce a report from a single version of
your design. To perform reference merging, use the -flex_merge reference switch as
follows:
urg -dir final_day.vdb merged.vdb -flex_merge reference
The switch considers only the coverage data that matches the reference version. If your
reference version has an 8-bit coverpoint in the covergroup, then only the data from the 8-
bit versions of that coverpoint are merged in the final report.
You should decide which merging strategy you should use early in the cycle and run test
merges to make sure it satisfies your requirements.

Overview
A typical verification project normally consists of four phases: planning with verification
intent, managing test runs, analyzing results, and converging on the coverage goals. Each
of these stages is an iterative process communicating with the others.
A well-designed coverage model combines different coverage technologies and metrics to
ensure all valid design scenarios are exercised and validated. The Verification Coverage
Flow (see Figure 1) drives the coverage model iteratively to tape out.
Figure 1 Figure 1: The Verification Coverage Flow
This document provides a basic introduction to using VCS coverage for design verification.
It discusses planning and coverage tools supported by VCS and suggests how the
different types of tools should be used together as part of an effective and comprehensive
coverage methodology. These guidelines should provide a starting point for new users,
while also serving as a handy reference for those experienced with planning and
coverage.
NOTE: For basic introduction to using VCS Coverage for design verification, see the
Using Coverage With VCS document under the Recommended Topics tab on the VCS
SolvNetPlus HTML page. The document discusses the planning and coverage tools
supported by VCS and suggests how the different types should be used together as part of
an effective and comprehensive coverage methodology.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Overview
Verification Planning
This document consists of the following sections:
• Verification Planning
• Obtaining Coverage Data for Your Design
• Code Coverage
• Functional Coverage
• Convergence
Verification Planning
A key part of planning is tying the original written specification and test plan documents to
corresponding verification goals. A linked, executable verification plan allows you to make
that connection.
Figure 2 shows how the specifications, plans, and data come together to track progress
and status. Links to the specifications ensure that every feature in the specification has
a corresponding feature in the plan. Links to verification data ensure that anything below
target (low coverage, tests failing, etc.) is presented and linked to the feature to highlight
needed action and owners.
Figure 2 Verification Specifications, Plans, and Data
The best way to create a verification plan is to start with the specification documents.
Create a top-level plan feature for each major feature in the specification, and then fill in
sub-features to match. At its most basic, the goal of a plan is to see which parts of the
project are on track and which need help, so dividing features into areas of responsibility is
a good way to start.
To create a plan from a PDF-format specification document, run Verdi coverage and open
your document. Highlight each major feature's introductory text and click one of the "create
feature" buttons in Verdi, to either create a sub-feature or a sibling feature. You can do the

Chapter 1: Overview
Obtaining Coverage Data for Your Design
same thing with the subsections of the major features. Identify sub-features that can be
verified separately, and then group them into parent features.
The next step is to connect measurable verification targets to the plan. The easiest way
to link coverage and other data sources into features is to run some simulations, open
the coverage databases in Verdi, and drag and drop the coverage regions from the Verdi
coverage window to each feature. Once you have linked those sources, whenever you
run Verdi or URG with a plan, the scores for linked features are automatically updated.
Alternately, you can create new measures inside each feature and specify the names
of the expected coverage sources. These names may be specified individually or using
wildcards.
The next section explains how to start collecting that coverage information.
Obtaining Coverage Data for Your Design
To obtain verification data for your design, you must compile your design and run
simulations.
It is important to use code coverage as early as possible in your verification process. It
does not have to be run often at this stage, but you can get early confirmation that the
metric types you have chosen are the right ones for you and that your merging, reporting,
and tracking setup works as desired.
This section consists of the following subsections:
• Compiling Design Files
• Running the Simulation
• Analyzing Coverage Results
Compiling Design Files
Some types of coverage, such as cover properties and covergroups, are automatically
enabled by the use of those structures in your design. Once you have defined them in your
design and testbench, coverage data for them is automatically collected whenever you run
a simulation.
Other coverage types require that you specify a corresponding option on the VCS
command line. For example, to compile your design for line coverage, add -cm line
when invoking VCS. For the complete list of coverage options, see "Compile Options for
Coverage Metrics" in Chapter 2, "Commands Reference" in the Coverage Technology
Reference Manual.

Chapter 1: Overview
Obtaining Coverage Data for Your Design
Running the Simulation
Metrics that must be specified on the command line are made available for collection in
your simulation executable, but are not collected unless you provide the corresponding
option when simulation is run. For example, to collect line coverage data, pass the -cm
line option on the simv command line. For the complete list of coverage options, see
"Simulation Options for Coverage Metrics" in Chapter 2, "Commands Reference" in the
Coverage Technology Reference Manual.
Analyzing Coverage Results
When compilation and simulation are done, VCS produces VDB directories containing
information about the coverage structures in the design and the coverage results from the
simulation runs.
To generate reports and analyze the results, use either of the following tools:
• Unified Report Generator (URG)
• Verdi Coverage GUI
Unified Report Generator (URG)
To invoke URG, specify one or more coverage database directories. The syntax to invoke
URG is as follows:
urg -dir dir1 [dir2 ] [urg_options]
where,
dir1 and dir2 are coverage database directories.
urg_options are URG command-line options.
For more information about URG options, see Chapter, "URG Options" in the
Coverage Technology Reference Manual.
Verdi Coverage GUI
To invoke the Verdi Coverage GUI, use the verdi command with the coverage command-
line option, -cov, and then load the coverage database directories. You can also specify
the directory name in the command-line via the -covdir option while invoking Coverage
GUI. The syntax to invoke the Verdi Coverage GUI is as follows:
verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Overview
Code Coverage
This command invokes Verdi in Coverage mode and loads the database. For more
information about the Verdi Coverage GUI, see Chapter, "Using Verdi Coverage" in the
Verdi Coverage User Guide and Tutorial.
Code Coverage
Code coverage provides a measure on how much of your design is exercised by the test
scenarios generated by the testbench. Code coverage monitors the following two basic
types of information:
1. Control-Flow Coverage tracks which lines and branches are considered during
simulation. This coverage monitors the flow of execution through each executable
statement in the SystemVerilog or VHDL code.
2. Value Coverage monitors what values signals and expressions take on during
simulation. Value-coverage metrics include condition coverage, toggle coverage, and
FSM coverage, which track the values (or value transitions) for signals and variables.
If you are not sure where to begin, it is recommended that you use the following VCS
compile-time options:
• For designs with a lot of procedural code:
Verilog behavioral code is inside procedure blocks (always and initial blocks).
VHDL procedural code is contained in processes.
For significant procedural code, use the following compile-time options:
-cm line+cond+fsm Specifies line, condition, and FSM coverage.
• For designs with less procedural code:
When there are more continuous assign statements in the design, use the following
compile-time options:
-cm line+branch+tgl Specifies line, branch, and toggle coverage.
-cm_line contassign Monitors continuous assignment statements.
In either case, it is recommended that to use the following option:
-cm_seqnoconst Automatically ignores constant expressions and flags
unreachable statements for line, toggle, and condition coverage.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 1: Overview
Functional Coverage
Functional Coverage
Functional coverage consists of two metric types: covergroups and cover properties/
assertions. Functional coverage is not automatically created from the HDL code. It
is explicitly created by you or IP vendors and specifically targeted to the intended
functionality or implementation of the design.
It is recommended to always use the following switch to improve performance of
immediate assertions during simulation:
vcs -assert fast_immediate …
One key distinction of functional coverage is that it is enabled by default. Disabling
functional coverage collection in some runs is sometimes desirable for performance.
Disabling functional coverage can be done separately for cover properties and
covergroups, as shown below:
simv -assert nocovdb //Disables cover property coverage
simv -covg_disable_cg //Disables covergroup coverage
Convergence
Any complex design may have code that is structurally unreachable or value combinations
that can never happen. As code coverage is automatically extracted from the HDL
description, there can many of these uninteresting or unreachable objects.
When you are trying to verify the design, you can exclude these impossible or do not-care
coverage targets so you can focus testing on the parts of the design that can happen.
The techniques to remove impossible or uninteresting parts of the design from coverage
monitoring are "Exclusion Management" and "Constant Analysis". For details on these two
techniques, see
Chapters, "Exclusion Management" and "Constant Analysis" respectively in the Coverage
Technology User Guide.

Overview
VCS® provides industry-leading coverage and planning capabilities for SystemVerilog,
VHDL, and mixed-language designs. A wide range of coverage metrics are available, with
detailed control available to users. The power and flexibility of VCS' coverage tools provide
support for many different coverage methodologies, but the range of options available may
be a bit overwhelming for new users.
This article provides a basic introduction to using VCS coverage for design verification.
It discusses the planning and coverage tools supported by VCS and suggests how
the different types should be used together as part of an effective and comprehensive
coverage methodology. These guidelines should provide a starting point for new users,
while also serving as a handy reference for those experienced with planning and
coverage.
The details of these features can be found in the VCS user documentation.
This document consists of the following topics:
• “Verification Planning”
• “Code Coverage”
• “Functional Coverage”
• “Managing Coverage Data Files”
• “Targeting Parts of Your Design”
• “Merging Coverage Data”
• “Generating Reports”
• “Convergence”
• “Test Grading”

Verification Planning
The purpose of planning is to create and maintain consistent links between the verification
specification and the tests, coverage and other data collected to provide actionable
information, organized by the plan specification, towards functional verification sign off. A
linked verification plan provides traceability from the specification details to the individual-
measured metric values.
The figure below shows how the specifications, plans, and data come together to
track progress and status. Links to the specifications ensure that every feature in the
specification has a corresponding feature in the plan. Links to verification data ensure
that anything below target (low coverage, tests failing, etc.) is presented and linked to the
feature to highlight needed action and owners.
The best way to create a verification plan is to start with the written specification
documents. Create a top-level plan feature for each major feature in the specification,
and then fill in sub-features to match. At its most basic, the goal of a plan is to see which
parts of the project are on track and which need help, so dividing features into areas of
responsibility is a good way to start.
To create a plan from a specification document, run Verdi coverage, and open your PDF
file. Highlight each major feature's introductory text and click one of the "create feature"
buttons in Verdi, to either create a sub-feature or a sibling feature. You can do the same
thing with the subsections of the major features. Identify sub-features that can be verified
separately, and then group them into parent features.

Chapter 2: Verification Planning

The easiest way to then link coverage sources into features is to drag and drop the
coverage regions from the Verdi coverage window to each feature. Once you have linked
coverage sources, whenever you run Verdi or URG with a plan, the coverage scores
for linked features are automatically updated. You can export the per-feature scores to
multiple formats from either tool.
If you want to link objects to the plan that do not yet exist in the database, you can enter
their names as sources in the plan. When they are added to the design in later iterations,
Verdi automatically finds them and annotates their scores in the design. For example, you
can use the name of a covergroup that will be written later as a source. You can also use
wildcard expressions, so if you have a naming convention for sources, you can have Verdi
automatically find any matching sources.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Code Coverage
When deciding what metrics and options to use, it is important to remember that each
metric has a cost - in simulation overhead, to some degree, but more importantly in
coverage closure overhead. Once you commit to a certain set of metrics, you are
committing the time it takes to develop tests, analyze results, apply waivers/ exclusions,
and, ultimately, reach your coverage goals.
There are two types of information that code coverage monitors. The first is control-flow
coverage that tracks which lines, paths, and branches are taken - the flow of execution
through each executable statement in the SystemVerilog or VHDL code. Control-flow
metrics include line coverage and branch coverage.
The second type is value coverage that monitors what values signals and expressions
take on during simulation. Value-coverage metrics include condition coverage, toggle
coverage, and FSM coverage, which track the values (or value transitions) for signals and
variables.
It is important to use code coverage as early as possible in your verification process. It
does not have to be run often at this stage, but you can get early confirmation that the
metric types you have chosen are the right ones for you and that your merging, reporting,
and tracking setup works as desired. It is better to have time to adjust your coverage flow
early on when you are not in crunch time.
If you are not sure where to begin, it is recommended to use the following VCS compile
options for designs with significant procedural code:
Compile Option Description
-cm line+cond+fsm Specifies line, condition, and FSM coverage.
-cm_cond obs+event Specifies observability-based condition coverage,
and conditions in always block sensitivity lists.
If your design has less procedural code, use the following compile options:
Compile Option Description
-cm line+branch+tgl Specifies line, branch, and toggle coverage.

Chapter 3: Code Coverage
Control-Flow Coverage
-cm_cond contassign Monitors whether continuous assignments ever wake
up during simulation
In either case, it is recommended to use the following options:
Compile Option Description
-cm_report noinitial Ignores initial blocks.
-cm_seqnoconst Automatically ignores constant expressions for
toggle and flag unreachable statements for line and
condition coverage. For more details, see Chapter 9,
"Convergence".
This chapter consists of the following sections:
• Control-Flow Coverage
• Value Coverage
Control-Flow Coverage
This section introduces each control-flow coverage metric briefly.
Line coverage is the most basic metric. It is a type of control-flow coverage, and monitors
which basic blocks in the design are executed during simulation. It is the best place to start
for most designs, to ensure that each block of code is at least being executed by testing.
Line coverage is invoked with the -cm line option.
It is recommended to use the -cm_report noinitial option to disable monitoring of line
coverage in SystemVerilog initial blocks. In addition, the -cm_line contassign option
enables line coverage on continuous assignments that have non-constant right-hand
sides.
Branch coverage tracks which branches are taken during simulation (if-then-else
branches, case statement items, and ternary operator choices). Branch coverage is only
concerned with whether each leaf in the control flow graph (the different sections of code
that can be executed depending on the value of signals and variables) is covered. Branch
coverage also does not monitor how each control-flow condition became true or false, as
condition coverage does.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 3: Code Coverage
Value Coverage
For example, in a ternary operator assignment such as the following there are three
branches to be covered, one for each of the three values that may be assigned to x (y,
z, and w):
x = a ? y : ( b ? z : w );
// branch 1: a is true, assign y
// branch 2: a is false and b is true, assign z
// branch 3: a and b are both false, assign w
In the next example, there are four branches (one for each of the true/false arms of the
two if statements).
if (a)
x <= 1'b0; // branch 1
else
x <= 1'b1; // branch 2
if (b)
y <= 1'b0; // branch 3
else
y <= 1'b1; // branch 4
Branch coverage is invoked with the -cm branch flag.
Value Coverage
Condition coverage measures which possible values each conditional expression
takes on during simulation. It is a hybrid of flow-control and value coverage. While
you can tell from line coverage that a given if statement is true (since the then part
executed), condition coverage tells you how the expression became true. For example, if
the expression is if (a || b) , condition coverage tells you whether a is ever true and
whether b is ever true, not just that (a || b ) is true. Condition coverage is invoked with
the -cm cond option.
It is recommended to use condition coverage with the -cm_cond obs option to enable
"observability-based" condition coverage. For nested expressions, such as if (a || (b
&& d)) ,
VCS tracks two expressions - the 'or' expression and the 'and' expression. When
-cm_cond obs is given, the 'and' expression is only monitored when the value of a is zero,
as the values of b and d have no effect on the result if a is true.
Finite-State Machine (FSM) coverage monitors which states, state transitions, and
sequence of states each finite-state machine in your design actually executed. VCS code
coverage automatically detects most FSMs, and you can modify how they are monitored,
such as specifying illegal states or transitions, using the FSM configuration file. For more
details about controlling and customizing how FSMs are monitored in your design, see the
Chapter, “More Options for FSM Coverage in the Coverage Technology Reference Guide.
FSM coverage is invoked with the -cm fsm option.

Chapter 3: Code Coverage
Value Coverage
It is recommended that you identify your reset signal(s) so that FSM coverage can reduce
the number of transitions it monitors. The -cm_fsmresetfilter flag allows you to specify
global or module- specific reset signals; when given, transitions that require reset to be
asserted are automatically ignored for coverage.
Toggle coverage monitors value changes on signal bits in the design. When toggle
coverage reaches 100%, it means that every bit of every monitored signal has changed its
value from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 0.
In SystemVerilog, to enable toggle coverage on elements in Multi- Dimensional arrays
(MDAs), use the -cm_tgl mda option to VCS. MDA coverage is not supported in VHDL
at this time. MDA toggle coverage monitoring can greatly increase the coverage space;
whether or not you use it depends on your design.
Depending on your design, toggle coverage can be one of the most expensive metrics in
simulation runtime. Some users prefer to only monitor the activity on port signals to reduce
the runtime overhead; you can do this with the compile-time option, -cm_tgl portsonly .
To invoke toggle coverage, use the -cm tgl option. For example:
% vcs -cm tgl -cm_tgl portsonly mydesign.v

Functional Coverage
Functional coverage consists of two metric types: covergroups and cover properties/
assertions. Functional coverage is not automatically discovered from the HDL code.
It is explicitly created by you or IP vendors and specifically targeted to the intended
functionality or implementation of the design.
Many books have been written on writing effective functional coverage, and we would not
presume to address that problem here. However, there are some VCS options and flows
that are useful to know about when using functional coverage.
One key distinction of functional coverage is that it is enabled by default. Because it is
only monitoring your design, however, you can turn it off without having any effect on
simulation. This is sometimes desirable for performance. Disabling functional coverage
can be done separately for cover properties and covergroups, as shown below:
simv -assert nocovdb //Disables cover property coverage
simv -covg_disable_cg //Disables covergroup coverage
This chapter consists of the following sections:
• Basic Rules for Covergroup Merging
• Covergroup Shapes in a Design
• Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Basic Rules for Covergroup Merging
If a module contains a covergroup instance, then each instance of the module has a
separate covergroup reported for it. For example, consider the following mymod module:
module mymod;
…
mygroup g1 = new(x, y, z);
endmodule
If there are three instances of mymod, they would each be reported separately:
top.a4b::addum
top.a4a::addum
top.a4c::addum

Covergroup Shapes in a Design
This separation ensures that just because a bin is covered in one instance, it does not
appear that the same testing has been done in the other instances.
To override this creation of multiple groups, use the URG option, -group
merge_across_scopes. This is useful when the goal of the group is explicitly to span the
behavior across all instances instead of tracking coverage separately for each instance
of the module. If this option is used, only a single covergroup is reported for all instances,
and, instead of using the instance name as a prefix, URG reports it as $unit(file),
where the file is the source file in which the group is defined:
$unit(test.v)::addum

Covergroup instances are also reported separately when their shapes are different. The
shape of a covergroup is determined by the number and size of each coverpoint and cross
in the group.

Covergroup Shapes in a Design
Covergroup instances are also reported separately when their shapes are different. The
shape of a covergroup is determined by the number and size of each coverpoint and cross
in the group.
Therefore, if a covergroup is passed a 4-bit argument in one case, and a 32-bit argument
in another, VCS splits it into two different shapes that are reported separately, even if they
are instantiated in the same scope.
When a covergroup is split into shapes this way, VCS uses the base name of the group
and adds the parameter values that differentiate the shapes. For example, if a parameter p
is used to determine the number of bins in a coverpoint, we might have the following in the
report:
$unit(test.v)::addum::SHAPE{p=16}
$unit(test.v)::addum::SHAPE{p=32}
There is no way to override this, as the different shapes cannot be merged in a meaningful
way.
Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
Another way that shape differences can arise is through changes to the covergroup
definition itself. For example, Monday version of a group may have 16 bins for one of its
coverpoints, but Tuesday version could have 32 bins for that coverpoint.
When this happens, by default URG keeps a separate copy of each different
version of each group that it finds in the coverage databases. For example, if

text:
Chapter 4: Functional Coverage
Covergroup Shape Changes Due to Edits
These have different detailed reports, with different numbers of bins and coverage data.
If you use the URG -show tests option (see the “Test Data” section), you can see which
tests covered any coverable bins in each version.
While it is not the default, the best option when the covergroup models are changing
frequently is to use the flexible merging options supported by VCS.
Flexible merging allows you to merge the data from the latest versions of your covergroup
models with the data collected from previous versions. In the flexible merging flow, you
can change the number of bins in a coverpoint, add or delete coverpoints, modify crosses,
and so on, and, still merge the data and retain a single covergroup that accumulates all
the data for the different versions.
The recommended flow is to use the -flex_merge union switch when accumulating your
coverage data (this switch has no effect on code coverage, so it is safe to use in a mixed
coverage environment, too). For example:
urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb … simvN.vdb -flex_merge union
-dbname merged.vdb -noreport
Union-merged databases contain multiple versions of coverpoints inside a given group.
The example below shows how union merge works when the size of a monitored register
changes from one version to the next. As coverpoint P does not change, its data is merged
normally. But the shape of coverpoint Q has changed, so we retain both versions in the
union merged result:
Version A Version B Merge Result
reg [3:0] Q;
reg [3:0] P;
covergroup G;
coverpoint P;
coverpoint Q;
endgroup
reg [7:0] Q;
reg [3:0] P;
covergroup G;
coverpoint P;
coverpoint Q;
endgroup
covergroup G;
coverpoint P;
coverpoint Q; (4 bits)
coverpoint Q; (8 bits)
endgroup
When ready to generate a report from a single version of your design - say at the end of
the week - you use a chosen reference design and use the -flex_merge reference
switch:
urg -dir Friday.vdb merged.vdb -flex_merge reference
This switch takes only the coverage data that matches the reference version. If your Friday
version has an 8-bit Q, then that is what you see in the report. As you used union merge,
you get the coverage data for coverpoint P from both versions of the group.
You should decide what merging strategy you should use early on and run test merges to
make sure it satisfies your needs.

text:
Managing Coverage Data Files
Using coverage produces some additional files and directories at compile and simulation
time. This section discusses how to manage the creation of those files, and how to merge
coverage data from multiple simulation runs.
When you compile with VCS, the executable name you specify determines the name of
the daidir created. For example:
vcs -o mysimv file1.v file2.v …
The above command creates a binary executable mysimv, and a corresponding
mysimv.daidir directory.
When coverage is enabled, the same name is used for creating the VDB directory, which
contains compile-time coverage-related information. For example, the following command
creates the mysimv.vdb directory, containing all compile-time coverage data:
vcs -cm line+cond+fsm -o mysimv file1.v file2.v …
There are other ways to name the mysimv.vdb directory, but it is recommended to let the
-o option determine the name to keep things consistent later.
Test Names
When you run simulations with coverage, you specify names for your coverage results.
These names are used to uniquely identify the sources of your coverage data at report
time.
The -cm_dir option, when given on the simv command line, specifies the directory in
which the runtime coverage results are saved. If you use this option, the runtime data
is written into a separate location from your compile-time data. Typically, users write the
results of every simv run to its own separate directory when each simv is submitted to a
grid/compute farm to be run in parallel.
The -cm_name flag is used to name the subdirectory in which the test data is stored. In
previous releases, this was the only name for the test data, and if you later moved the
parent VDB directory, it changed the name of the test. The argument you give to -cm_name
needs to be unique within the targeted VDB directory or the data from the latest run
overwrites the data from the previous run with the same -cm_name.

Chapter 5: Managing Coverage Data Files
Test Names
For example, to run two sets of tests, run1 and run2, and save the data for each set into
its own VDB directory, use the following:
mysimv -cm_dir t1dir.vdb -cm_name t1 …
mysimv -cm_dir t1dir.vdb -cm_name t2 …
mysimv -cm_dir t2dir.vdb -cm_name t1 …
mysimv -cm_dir t2dir.vdb -cm_name t2 …
These commands result in two VDB directories, each containing two tests. For example, if
these directories are under /proj/march/run7, the test names would be:
/proj/march/run7/t1dir/t1
/proj/march/run7/t1dir/t2
/proj/march/run7/t2dir/t1
/proj/march/run7/t2dir/t2

Targeting Parts of Your Design
At compile time, you can tell VCS to monitor code coverage for only parts of your design,
for example, to ignore external IP when monitoring coverage. You can also choose to
apply different metrics on different blocks.
Even if you collect coverage for the entire design, you can do the same kind of filtering at
report time. Both of these features are based on a 'hier' file.
A hier file consists of a sequence of + and - directives. A + directive includes the specified
target or region, and a - directive excludes it. If the first directive is for inclusion, it implies
that everything else is excluded. Similarly, if the first directive is exclusion, it means that
everything else in the design is included.
Each directive has a keyword following the + or - symbol. The supported keywords include
the following:
Keyword Meaning
tree Specifies a subtree in the design hierarchy.
module Specifies a specific module.
moduletree Specifies a subtree of a specific module, everywhere it is
instantiated.
node Specifies a specific signal.
assert Specifies an assertion or cover property.
library Specifies a library.
file Specifies a specific source file.
For example, a hier file consisting of the following line means that only this tree is
monitored for any type of coverage:
+tree top.HNTO_0.HNWOV_0

Chapter 6: Targeting Parts of Your Design

Whereas, the following in the hier file means that everything should be monitored except
for the specified module:
-module Wovmod
These hier files can be used at either compile time or report time. When used at
compile time, in some cases they can improve simulation performance, as coverage
instrumentation can be removed. You can also specify that only certain metrics be
collected or excluded from regions of the design. For more details, see the Coverage
Technology Reference Guide.

Merging Coverage Data
After running multiple simulation runs, the next step is to merge all the coverage data from
those runs. Once the data is merged, you can generate reports or load the merged data
into Verdi to analyze the results.
Merging is done with the urg command. To merge data, you need to provide the compile-
time VDB directory and then any simulation- produced VDB directories. The basic merge
command is as follows:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t1dir.vdb t2dir.vdb … -dbname merged
-noreport
This command reads all of the specified VDB directories and merges them to create a
new VDB named merged.vdb. The -noreport switch indicates that we do not want to
generate a report at the same time (it is better to generate reports separately).
You probably do not want to do a serial merge of all your coverage data, as merging is an
inherently parallelizable process. You can direct URG to do the merging in parallel, either
on a single machine, on multiple machines, or on a compute farm/grid. The basic option
to add is -parallel. To see the flags for different supported grid types, see the Coverage
Technology Reference Guide.
There are many different options to direct how merging works. We discussed some
functional coverage merging options in Section Basic Rules for Covergroup Merging .
There are a couple of other major merging options worth considering for your flow.

• Mapping
• Test Data

design.

Mapping
Mapping is what URG calls for merging the coverage results from different subsets of the
design. A common use of mapping is to merge the coverage results collected for a sub-
block onto the SOC coverage model of the full design. For example, the coverage for the

md3 block in the figure below is merged onto all instances of its top module in the base
design using the URG -map option:
When mapping, the coverage of any unmapped modules, such as tbblk in this example,
is ignored. This allows you to peel off the testbench from a block and just copy the design
coverage.
The default -map option is simple and module-based. To perform more sophisticated
mapping on an instance-by-instance basis, use the -mapfile option.
Test Data
By default, URG retains the list of all test records in the final merged VDB. Using the
example from Section, “Test Names” , there are two test records in each of t1dir.vdb and
t2dir.vdb.To merge these two records together, use the following command:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -dbname merged -noreport
The newly-created merged.vdb directory contains test records for the following:
/run1/test1
/run1/test2
/run2/test1
/run2/test2
These test records retain data such as simulation cycles, peak memory use, and CPU
time, etc. If you specify pass/fail status or other annotations to the test records, they are
also retained.

Chapter 7: Merging Coverage Data
Test Data
By default, URG does not keep track of which test covered which object in the merged
VDB. Once the merged VDB is created, you can still see which objects are covered,
but by default you cannot see which tests are responsible. To retain this test correlation
information, you must also provide the -show tests switch when created the merged
VDB:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -dbname merged -noreport
-show tests
This command increases the size of merged.vdb - as more information is saved now -
but it also allows you to generate reports with -show tests that show the tests that cover
each object:
% urg -dir merged.vdb -show tests …
We do not retain every test name that covered every object. It does not make sense to
keep track of every test that caused your clock to toggle, for example. You can change the
maximum number of tests saved per covered object using the -db_max_tests option:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -dbname merged -noreport \
-show tests -db_max_tests 20
Retaining the test correlation data has another benefit - you can do test grading on the
merged VDB. In previous releases, you had to keep all the simulation-time VDBs to
perform grading.

Generating Reports
You generate a report by passing the names of all directories containing coverage data
to URG's -dir option. The first directory passed should be compile-time directories. For
example:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb
By default, URG generates its reports in HTML in the urgReport directory. To get started,
open urgReport/dashboard.html with your web browser. URG's HTML reports support
many interactive options including expanding and collapsing regions and navigation
panes. You can also generate text-format reports using the -format text command line
option.

• Metrics

• Trend Charts

Metrics
If you want to report only certain metrics, use the -metric flag:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -metric line+group
Ratios
There are many options that affect how the report is generated and how scores are
computed. The -hier option to URG is already discussed in Chapter Chapter 6,

Chapter 8: Generating Reports
Trend Charts
"Targeting Parts of Your Design". It is also recommended to use the -show ratios option.
This option has two effects:
• Reports show the number of covered and coverable objects for each metric, instead of
just the percentage score.
• This option causes URG to compute the covergroup score as the ratio of (number of
covered bins) / (number of bins). This is not the LRM-defined scoring method, but the
ratio scoring is preferred because the LRM scoring algorithm results in artificially-high
coverage scores when the coverage can still be very low.
Verdi has corresponding preferences that you can set to achieve the same results.
Trend Charts
If you save the urgReport directories produced over a period of time, you can use them to
generate graphical trend reports of how coverage is changing over time. The URG -trend
option generates these hyperlinked reports. If you are using a verification plan, the charts
include the scores of plan features. If you have stored your saved urgReports in the /
u/fred/myreports directory, the basic usage is as follows:
% urg -trend root /u/fred/myreports
URG then generates a trend chart that you can load in your browser. For more on trend
charts, see the Coverage Technology User Guide.
Navigating Coverage Reports
URG generates a dashboard report that is a good place to start. This includes the rolled-
up coverage scores for all top-level instances, and the overall score across the whole
design. The hierarchy report is an interactive HTML report (or static text report) that lets
you see the rolled-up scores at any level of the hierarchy. Covergroups are listed in the
groups report, and assertions and cover properties have their own assertions report. Every
URG HTML report page has a common link menu at the top that you can use to navigate:
From any page that displays module or instance names, you can click on those names
and be taken to the detailed coverage report for that region.

text:
Convergence
Any complex design may have code that is structurally unreachable, or value
combinations that can never happen. As code coverage is automatically extracted from
the HDL description, there can many of these uninteresting or unreachable objects.
When you are trying to verify the design, you have to exclude these impossible or do not-
care coverage targets so you can focus testing on the parts of the design that can happen.
This section explains some ways to remove impossible or uninteresting parts of the design
from coverage monitoring.
Exclusion is complementary to the 'hier' file flow discussed in Chapter 6, "Targeting Parts
of Your Design". Exclusion is typically targeted more at individual objects, while the hier file
flow is used to address regions of the design.
This chapter consists of the following sections:
• Constant Analysis
• Adaptive Exclusion
Constant Analysis
Start with VCS' built-in constant analysis feature. You should always use the
-cm_seqnoconst switch if you are using code coverage:
% vcs -cm_seqnoconst -cm line+cond+tgl file1.v file2.v …
The -cm_seqnoconst switch automatically searches for structurally unreachable coverage
targets and removes them from the coverage target list. These objects appear in the
coverage reports grayed-out, with the word 'unreachable'.
Sometimes these unreachable objects are not intended to be unreachable by designers.
To help understand the unreachability analysis, VCS supports a diagnostic switch, -diag:
% vcs -cm_seqnoconst -diag noconst -cm line+cond+tgl file1.v
…
When this switch is given, the constfile.txt file is created at compile time that lists
all signals and parts of signals that VCS found to be constant, with an explanation for
each one. The explanation gives the expression that was found to be constant, where

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
Chapter 9: Convergence
Adaptive Exclusion
it is declared, where it is assigned, and the list of other signal parts that are found to be
constant that are assigned to it. For example, in the snippet of the constfile.txt file
below, the expression attention[9:5] in the test_jukebox.jb1 instance is found to
always be 0, and it is assigned hold[4:0] at line 899 :
- instance: test_jukebox.jb1
expression: attention[9:5]
declaration: jukebox.v:436
value: 0 always
locations:
- location: jukebox.v:899
inputs:
- input: hold[4:0]
Synopsys also provides formal analysis tools that can further improve on the constant
analysis done by VCS under the -cm_seqnoconst switch. VCS's built-in "noconst"
analysis complements the formal tools by finding the easier-to-find unreachable let the
formal tools focus on the more difficult cases.
Adaptive Exclusion
When performing coverage analysis, it is recommended to perform the analysis in Verdi.
When you identify a coverage target that can be ignored, or is impossible by design,
you can mark it for exclusion directly in the GUI and add a comment explaining why it
is excluded. You can then save those exclusions and comments to an exclude file that
can be reused in the next and future sessions. Excluded objects are removed from the
coverage score calculation and appear grayed out in reports.
To exclude lines from coverage, for example, you click the green circle next to them in the
Coverage Details pane. After excluding objects, you then click the Recalculate button in
Verdi, which updates the coverage scores. The snapshot below shows that line 247 is
excluded and the Recalculate button is clicked:
A common flow for exclusions is to load exclude files created in previous sessions and
then to do further analysis and exclusions. When you are ready to save your progress, you
can save only the newly-created exclusions, to a separate file. This lets you keep the new
exclusions separate until they can be reviewed by the team, for example. You can also
choose to save excludes for different metrics separately, save the exclusions only for a
specific block, module or covergroup, and so on. You should establish your team's exclude
file management policy before you begin coverage convergence.

Chapter 9: Convergence
Adaptive Exclusion
The example below shows Verdi's Exclusion Manager pane. In this pane, you can see
a flat list of all exclusions applied to the current design, along with descriptions and any
comments (annotations) that are added. Clicking on any exclusion brings up the coverage
details and source window so you can examine the object in context.
It is recommended to use the Exclusion Manager flat view (a hierarchical view is also
available) to conduct exclusion reviews with your team.
The most important feature of the exclusion flow is that it is able to remap most exclusions
from one version of your design to the next. Fundamentally, your team spends a large
amount of effort deciding what objects can safely be excluded, and a design change that
does not affect an exclusion should not make you re-analyze it.
This is why Verdi preserves your exclusions as-is when the design changes, without
intervention, unless the object being monitored or the control code around it has changed.
And for exclusions whose objects have changed, Verdi Exclusion Manager walks you
through each one so you can decide if the exclusions still apply, or tell Verdi what if
anything needs to change.
Once an exclude file is generated, you can load it into Verdi interactively, or you can apply
it to a URG report using the -elfile option as shown below:
% urg -dir simv.vdb -elfile blk1.el …

Test Grading
Grading, or test ranking, means comparing the effectiveness of tests for coverage.
Grading is useful when you want to eliminate redundant tests from a test suite or put tests
in best-first order.
Grading can select tests based purely on coverage score, minimizing the total number of
tests required to hit the coverage score hit by the whole database, or it can be directed
to select tests to minimize total CPU time, simulation cycles, or wall clock time. The basic
grading command - assuming you used -show tests when created your merged VDB - is
shown below:
% urg -dir merged.vdb -grade listonly
To grade to minimize total CPU time instead, use the following command:
% urg -dir merged.vdb -grade cost cputime listonly
If you did not use -show tests when creating your merged VDB, or you have merged yet
at all, you can use the -parallel switch to do a parallel merge and then grade the tests:
% urg -dir mysimv.vdb t*dir.vdb -grade listonly -parallel
Some useful options for grading are given in the table below. Provide these options
anywhere after the "-grade" option on the URG command line:
Options Description
indexlimit N Retains at most N tests per covered object. Higher N uses more memory
and time but produces more precise grading results
cost [cputime|simtim
e|clocktime]
Grades tests to minimize the total cost (CPU time, simulation cycles, or
clock time) instead of minimizing the number of tests
testfile Generates a file 'gradedtests.txt' in the urgReport directory that is a
simple list of the graded tests, in order.
