Compiling and Linking the SystemC Source Files
You can decide how and when to compile your source files with GCC. However, you must
use the following GCC flags during compilation:
• Use the SystemC headers from VCS image: g++ -I$VCS_HOME/include/systemc233
…
Or use SystemC 233, 234 or any other supported version. Do not use headers files
from OSCI/Accellera.
• Always add the -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 option. This macro is used in some areas to
distinguish VCS-SystemC from OSCI/Accellera or other third-party SystemC kernels.
• Always use the -fPIC option, which GCC requires for a shared library
• Use -m32 for 32-bit and -m64 for 64-bit simulation.
• Compile the SystemC source file with the debug information ( g++ -g … ) in the
following scenarios:
◦ You want to instantiate the SystemC model in Verilog or VHDL (SC-down interface
model).
◦ You want TLI capabilities for the SystemC model.

Shared Library Flow
◦ You want full debug support for the SystemC model with Verdi or UCLI.
Most of the SystemC/HDL glue requires to know the internals of the SystemC
model which VCS gets from the debug information that GCC creates with -g.
• It is recommended to use both the -g and -O GCC flags, which provides the necessary
debug information and also optimized object code that runs faster: g++ -g -O …
However, you must omit the -O flag when you plan to perform interactive debugging
because stepping through optimized GCC code tends to be confusing.
1. Set the GCC flags using the following commands:
% g++ -c … -fPIC -m32 -g -O -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -I$VCS_HOME/
include/systemc233 A.cpp
% g++ -c … -fPIC -m32 -g -O -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -I$VCS_HOME/
include/systemc233 B.cpp
2. Link all the object files into a shared library using the following syntax:
% g++ -shared -o libSC.so A.o B.o
3. Add the shared library to the VCS elaboration command:
% vcs … libSC.so …
You can also use other methods to specify the shared library. For example, with
the -ldflags, -L or -l options. Set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH as necessary. For more
information, see VCS documentation.
Ensure that use the exact same GCC version that was used to compile your SystemC
source files. It is possible to use multiple shared libraries for your SystemC and other C/C+
+ source files.
Using Makefiles
Makefiles enable you to get all your SystemC source files compiled into a shared library.
You can configure a Makefile using the compile flags as described in the previous section.
A sample makefile is as follows:
SRC = A.cpp B.cpp

CXX = g++
CXXFLAGS = -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -m32 -fPIC -g -O \
-I$(VCS_HOME)/include/systemc233-I$(VCS_HOME)/include/systemc233
OBJS = $(SRC:%.cpp=%.o)
%.o: %.cpp $(DEPS)

Shared Library Flow
$(CXX) -c -o $@ $< $(CXXFLAGS)

libSC.so: $(OBJS)
$(CXX) -o $@ -shared -m32 $(OBJS)

clean:
rm -f $(OBJS)
rm -f $(subst .o,.d,$(OBJS))
rm -fr libSC.so
Generating an SC/HDL Interface model
To create an SC-down interface model, use the shared library instead of a source file
using the following syntax:
% syscan libSC.so:A [other syscan options]
Note that the source code containing SC_MODULE(A) must have been compiled with the
debug information (g++ -g ), if not syscan is not able to locate that model.
Specify other options in the similar method as you do for syscan A.cpp:A .
For example, -Mlib=… or -sysc=opt_if .
If you plan to perform interactive debug, then compile with debug information:
% syscan libSC.so:A -cflags -g
HDL Connect
The hdl_connect is used to connect SystemC objects (sc_signals) to Verilog/
VHDL objects, so that value changes on either side propagates to the other side. The
hdl_connect is Synopsys' way of connecting SystemC to HDL simulators, and should
only be used with a Synopsys simulator.
defined in $VCS_HOME/include/cosim/bf/hdl_connect.h
template < class T >
void hdl_connect(sc_signal<T> &sig,
const char *hdl_signal,
hdl_direction d,
int simid)
- sc_signal<T> &sig : a reference to the SystemC signal to
which it is hooked
- const char *hdl_signal : a full pathname of the HDL object
- hdl_direction d : Signal direction:

Support for syscan in Parallel Build Environment
Using the SNPS_SYSC_MODULE_EXPORT Macro
When GCC links the shared library, it sometimes skips one or more SystemC modules
because they are apparently unused. Creating an SC/HDL interface model fails in this
case and syscan states that no module “A” is defined.
To avoid this issue, add the SNPS_SYSC_MODULE_EXPORT macro in the relevant SystemC
source file (*.cpp).
File A.h:
SC_MODULE(A) {
…
};

Support for syscan in Parallel Build Environment
VCS supports parallel analysis flow in designs that contain SystemVerilog/VHDL and
SystemC files. This specifically prevents the read/write conflicts of SystemC related files
created during syscan calls that are issued in parallel within the same working directory.
Though SystemC related analysis and I/O file of syscan, vlogan -sc_model, and vhdlan
-sc_model are internally serialized, vlogan, vhdlan calls unrelated to SystemC calls are
parallelized. Thus, accelerating the analysis phase. There is no change in the use model
for compiling and running designs that have SystemVerilog, VHDL, and SystemC files.
• Parallel elaboration in the same working directory is not supported.
For example, vcs TOP -o simv1 …
• Clock time spent on SystemC related analysis calls (that is, syscan or vlogan,
-sc_model or vhdlan -sc_model ) does not reduce as the SystemC related analysis
calls are internally serialized.

Elaboration Scheme
• Ensure that the logical dependencies between analysis calls are executed sequentially.
(1) vlogan bottom.v -sc_model bottom // creates bottom.h
(2) syscan top.cpp // #include "bottom.h"
The top.cpp file need bottom.h, which is generated by step 1. As this is logically
dependent, execute step 2 only after step 1 is completed.
• Two-step flow is not supported (For example, vcs A.v …; syscsim … ). This
enhancement is only supported with the UUM flow.
Elaboration Scheme
When SystemC is at the top of the design hierarchy, you can instantiate Verilog code in the
SystemC code. The elaboration of the simulation is performed in the following two steps:
1. First, VCS creates a temporary simulation executable. This executable contains all
SystemC parts, but does not yet contain any HDL (Verilog, VHDL, ) parts. VCS
then starts this temporary executable to find out which Verilog/VHDL instances
are needed. All SystemC constructors, begin_end_of_elaboration() and
end_of_elaboration() methods are executed during this step. However, simulation
does not start at this point. Information about SystemC or HDL instances is extracted
and stored for the next step.
2. VCS creates the final version of the simv file containing SystemC, and all HDL parts.
The design is now fully elaborated and ready to simulate.
As a side effect of executing the temporary executable during step 1, all
statements located inside the constructors are executed. Statements inside
begin_end_of_elaboration()and end_of_elaboration() methods are also executed.
Additionally, all statements inside sc_main up to the first sc_start() call are executed.
If your simulation contains statements that should not be executed during step 1, you need
to guard these statements. You can use a check for the SYSTEMC_ELAB_ONLY environment
variable or, with the following function:
extern "C" bool hdl_elaboration_only()
Both are set/yield true only during this extra execution of simv during step 1.
For example, guard the statements as follows:
sc_main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
// instantiate signals, modules,
ModuleA my_top_module(); // <-- must always be executed

if (! hdl_elaboration_only())
{
open log file for simulation report
}

sc_start(); // <-- must always be executed
if (! hdl_elaboration_only())
{
close log file

}
If you guard the statements as mentioned earlier, ensure that all the module constructors
are executed. Also, ensure that at least one call of sc_start() is executed.
VCS needs to know the entire SystemC module hierarchy during step 1. This means that
all SystemC constructors must be executed.
If your simulation checks the command line arguments argc and argv, then you have the
following two options:
• Guard these statements with an IF-statement as shown above.
Or
• Provide the simv command line arguments used during elaboration using the VCS
argument -syscelab. For example,
vcs -sysc sc_main -syscelab A
You can specify the -syscelab option multiple times. White space within the arguments
is not preserved. Instead, the arguments are broken up into multiple arguments. Multiple
arguments can also be enclosed within double quotes. For example, you can use
-syscelab "1 2 3".
If your SystemC design topology (the set of SystemC instances) depends on simv runtime
arguments, you must provide the relevant arguments with -syscelab. The SystemC
design topology during step 1 must be identical during the final execution of simv .
Note that, the -syscelab option is only supported when SystemC is at the top of the
design hierarchy. If Verilog or VHDL is at the top, then -syscelabis neither required nor
supported.

Introduction to Precompiled Header Files
The precompiled header files
systemc.h
systemc.h and systemc must be generated before you
use them. The
g++
g++ compiler first searches for a precompiled header file in the specified
include paths. In case it finds the header file, the g++ compiler uses the matching
precompiled header file. If not, it parses the specified header file (ASCII version) as usual.
A nonmatch can be caused by the use of different compile options. For example, use
options like
-m32
-m32 or
–fPIC
-m32 -fPIC . This issue occurs while creating the precompiled header
file and the g++ call.
Using Precompiled Header Files
Use the syscan option to create precompiled header files (systemc.h and systemc).
Compile the given SystemC files. Add a search path to the location of the precompiled
header file:
%syscan -prec[=<target_directory>] <file1>[<file2>]
•
target_directory
<target_directory> is the user-specified path. If specified, this path is the first path
searched for all includes.
• <file1>, <file2> are the SystemC source files.
The earlier mentioned command creates the precompiled header files
systemc.h and systemc, if these do not exist. Otherwise, it uses the
precompiled header files that are already present.

Improving Compilation Speed Using Precompiled C++ Headers
If you mention <target_directory>, then the g++ call first searches this directory for
precompiled header files. This ensures that you get the best performance improvement,
and that the precompiled header files are used if they exist.
If you do not specify a directory, g++ creates a precompiled header file in each of the
following two directories:
./csrc/sysc/prec/$hostname/<SC_version>/<GCC_version>/<VCS_version>/syste
mc_.h.gch/

./csrc/sysc/prec/$hostname/<SC_version>/<GCC_version>/<VCS_version>/syste
mc_.gch/
The file name is based on the compile-time options (for example, m32_fPIC for -m32
-fPIC).
If -Mdir is specified as an argument to syscan -prec , then the directory structure
appears as follows:
<mdir_path>/prec/$hostname/<SC_version>/<GCC_version>/<VCS_version_id>/sy
stemc_.h.gch/
and
<mdir_path>/prec/$hostname/<SC_version>/<GCC_version>/<VCS_version_id>/sy
stemc_.gch/
Specify a directory name with the -prec option to generate precompiled header files
in prec/systemc_.h.gch/and in prec/systemc_.gch/ within that directory. If you
use -Mdir with -prec with a path, the
-Mdir
-Mdir option is ignored for the location of the
precompiled headers.
The generation of the precompiled header files is done using makefiles. In case of no
change, a precompiled header file is not generated again.
The following example shows how to use precompiled header files:
In this example, assume that a Verilog module my_top instantiates a SystemC module
called my_sc_top.
% syscan -prec -tlm2 my_sc_top.cpp:my_sc_top
This command creates the precompiled header files:
% syscan -prec my_sc_module.cpp

Improving Compilation Speed Using Precompiled C++ Headers
These commands use the precompiled header files created by the above command:
% vlogan -sverilog my_top.sv
% vcs -sysc my_top
Invoking the Creation of Precompiled Header Files
If any of the following changes occur, syscan -prec triggers creation of the appropriate
precompiled header files.
• The GCC version is different from the one used for the creation of the precompiled
header files systemc.h and/or systemc .
• Compile flags are not the same.
• SystemC-related defines passed with -D as argument(s) of the -cflags option are not
the same.
• $VCS_HOME (version) changes.
• SystemC version changes.
• Host changes (different system include files).
If the -prec option is called with a user-specified path, then a sanity check is done. This
ensures that the precompiled header files are already generated at the specified location.
If any of the previously mentioned changes occur, an appropriate message is generated.
and the creation and usage of precompiled header files is skipped. This occurs for VCS,
GCC, SystemC version, and host name changes.

This section lists the limitations that apply to the following:
• Limitations of GNU Precompiled Header Files
• Limitations of syscan -prec Option

Improving Compilation Speed Using Precompiled C++ Headers
Limitations of GNU Precompiled Header Files
• The option used for creating the precompiled header file and the actual object file must
be the same. If not, the precompiled header file is skipped.
• Only one precompiled header file can be used in one compilation step.
• Any C token before a precompiled header file is skipped.
• The g++ compiler installation to create the precompiled header file and the actual g++
compiler installation must be the same.
• Any macro defined before the precompiled header file must be the same when creating
and using it.
Limitations of syscan -prec Option
• The include statement of a SystemC header file must be on top of a file. Any C/C++
token used before the SystemC header file skips the usage of the precompiled header
file. This also parses the ASCII source file.
A C/C++ token can be any valid C/C++ source code like a typedef or variable
declaration. Preprocessor directives (for example, #define, #include) are not
C/C++ tokens.
• Two precompiled header files are created, one for systemc.h and one for systemc.
• The size of a precompiled header file is at least 2.5 MB. The size depends on the
options passed in a sysc -prec call.
• All syscan calls must use the -prec option to make use of the precompiled header
files.
• A change in compile flags and/or SystemC related defines in a syscan -prec call
creates precompiled header files with those settings.
• If you use SystemC-related defines before a SystemC header file, create the
precompiled SystemC header file with the same defines names and values. Use the -D
option as part of -cflags in the syscan -prec command.
The defines in front of a SystemC header file must match the set of defines used in the
precompiled header file creation step. If matching precompiled files are not found, then
the ASCII version of the SystemC header file is used.

Limitations of Using -prec With Path
This feature has the following limitation:
• If there are already precompiled header files stored in the path-location, a sanity
check is done with respect to changes to hostname, SystemC version , gcc version ,
and VCS version (time stamp).
If one of these does not match, a warning message is generated, and the creation (and
usage) of the precompiled header files is skipped. The result is that the precompiled
header files are not used in the compile step. Putting the host name as part of the path
prevents skipping (and usage) of precompiled header files in case of any host name
changes. All the rest must match.
Limitations of Sharing Precompiled Header Files
• You must call the
-prec
-prec option, along with an absolute path, to share precompiled
header files. You must have read (and maybe write) permissions.
If there is a change with respect to the name of the host, then VCS, GCC, and
SystemC version sharing is not possible. In this case, the sanity check creates a
warning, and the usage of precompiled header files is skipped.
In most cases, the name of the host changes. If the host name is part of the path (such
as, /some_dir/${hostname}/), then the precompiled header files can be used. The
downside is that the precompiled header files are created in this specific directory with
the information used by VCS, SystemC, and GCC version.
• You must call the syscan executable with the -prec option with the same path. Any
change in the compile flags (passed with -cflags) invokes the creation of precompiled
header files, if they do not exist for the changed combination of compile flags.
Modeling SystemC Designs With SCV
You can model your designs containing SystemC and SystemC Verification Standard
(SCV) using VCS. The following features are explained in this section:
• SCV Library in VCS
• msglog Extensions for Transaction Recording With SCV in VCS

Modeling SystemC Designs With SCV
SCV Library in VCS
The SCV library is shipped along with the VCS image. SCV library is supported for all
SystemC versions for all the compilers. SCV library is not binary compatible with OSCI-
SystemC, but belongs to the SystemC version shipped with VCS.
The VCS- SystemC flow supports the following SCV versions:
• SCV 1.0p2 (default version)
• SVC 2.0
For the SCV version and its compatible version of GCC compiler, see the VCS Release
Notes.
• To select the default SCV version (1.0p2), you can use the -sysc=scv option on
syscan while compiling the source code containing SCV. This option adds the
required include directories within the VCS image during analysis. Also, use the
-sysc=scvoption on VCS command that selects the correct library to be linked.
syscan -sysc=scv myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv
You can also use -sysc=scv10 option instead of -sysc=scv option, as both these
options exhibit the same functionality.
syscan -sysc=scv10 myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv10
• To select SCV 2.0 version, you can use the -sysc=scv20 option on syscan.
syscan -sysc=scv20 myfile.cpp
vcs -sysc -sysc=scv20
It is not allowed to integrate SCV 1.0p2 and SCV 2.0 versions with the same
simulation. You must use the same version consistently throughout all the
calls of syscan and VCS.

Modeling SystemC Designs With SCV
msglog Extensions for Transaction Recording With SCV in VCS
VCS provides a capability to record SCV transactions using msglog. SCV provides
callbacks, which are implemented to record the transactions during the following calls:
• begin_transaction()
• end_transaction()
• record_attribute()
You can view the SCV transactions in Verdi waveform window using this feature. The
callback functions provided by SCV, which are executed when the methods listed earlier
mentioned are called are implemented in VCS. This way you do not need to write any
custom code to record the SCV transactions in MSGLOG apart from registering the callback
functions implemented in VCS.
You must register the callback functions implemented in VCS. Since these callback
functions are declared in vcs_scv_callback.h file, you must include this file before
registering these functions. The source file must be compiled with the -sysc=scvoption,
as these functions are a part of the SCV library.
#include "vcs_scv_callback.h"
scv_tr_handle::callback_h tr_handle1, tr_handle2;
//registering the call back function for recording the begin and end attributes
tr_handle1 = scv_tr_handle::register_class_cb(&vcs_scv_callback);
//registering the call back function for recording the special attributes
tr_handle2 =
scv_tr_handle::register_record_attribute_cb(&vcs_scv_callback_record_att
ribute);
syscan -sysc=scv main.cpp
By default, all the transactions are recorded in the same stream, assuming that the
second transaction starts only after finishing the first transaction, and so on. If there
are overlapping transactions in your SCV testbench (second transaction starting even
before first transaction is finished), then compile your source code along with the
-DSNPS_MSGLOG_OVERLAP=1 define on syscan. This way, transactions are recorded in
multiple streams.

Controlling TimeScale and Resolution
Controlling TimeScale and Resolution
The HDL (Verilog, VHDL) kernel and the SystemC kernel of VCS have individual settings
for time resolution. These values must be the same, otherwise a runtime warning or error
occurs. The difference may slow down the simulation, lead to wrong simulation results,
or even make the simulation be "stuck" at one time point and not progress. It is therefore,
highly recommended to ensure that time resolution from both kernels have the same
settings.
The SystemC runtime kernel has a timescale and time resolution that can be controlled
using the following functions:
• sc_set_time_resolution()
• sc_set_default_time_unit()
This section explains how to achieve same time resolution for both HDL and SystemC
kernel.
Setting TimeScale/Resolution of Verilog/VHDL Kernel
The most convenient way to ensure that Verilog/VHDL and SystemC use
the same timescale or resolution is using the VCS -timescale=1ns/1ps or
-override_timescale=1ns/ps command-line options.
% vcs -sysc top -timescale=1ns/1ps
This command forces the Verilog/VHDL kernel to have the same values as the default
values from the SystemC kernel. If this is not possible (for example, because you need
a higher resolution in a Verilog module), then you can change the default values of the
SystemC kernel as described in the following section.
Setting TimeScale/Resolution of SystemC Kernel
The default timescale of a SystemC kernel is 1 ns, and the default time resolution is 1
ps. These default are not affected by the VCS -timescale option. To control the time
resolution of the SystemC module, create a static global object that initializes the timing
requirements for the module. This can be a separate file that is included as one of the
.cpp files for the design.
Sample contents for this file are as follows:
class set_time_resolution
{

Controlling TimeScale and Resolution
set_time_resolution()
{
try
{
sc_set_time_resolution(10, SC_PS);
}
catch( const sc_exception& x )
{
cerr << "setting time resolution failed: " <<
x.what() << endl;
}
}
};

static int SetTimeResolution()
{
new set_time_resolution();
return 42;
}
static int time_resolution_is_set = SetTimeResolution();
Automatic Adjustment of Time Resolution
If the time resolution of SystemC and HDL differs, VCS can also automatically determine
the finer time resolution and set it as the simulator’s timescale. To enable this feature, you
must use the -sysc=adjust_timeres elaboration option.
vcs -sysc -sysc=adjust_timeres
Note that, VCS may not be able to adjust the time resolution if you elaborate your HDL
with the -timescale option and/or use the sc_set_time_resolution() function call in
your SystemC code. In such cases, VCS reports an error and does not create simv.
When the -sysc=adjust_timeres option is used, during the elaboration phase, a partial
simulation is launched and is immediately stopped at time 0.
This partial simulation might fail unexpectedly. The following are some of the possible
reasons for the failure.
• A SEGV/crash in the C++ user code.
• If the sc_main() function is present and returns with a status other than 0.
• The argc/argv arguments are not correct.

Adding a Main Routine for Verilog-On-Top Designs
Error-[SC-VCS-SYSC-ELAB] SystemC elaboration error
The design could not be fully elaborated due to an early termination of
the SystemC part of the design.
Read the hints in file simv.README or review the details in the SystemC
chapter of the VCS documentation.
• The -sysc=adjust_timeres option is not supported in two-step flow. It is only
supported in three-step (UUM) flow.
• If there is a mismatch in the time resolution, compile time may increase with the
-sysc=adjust_timeres option. Therefore, it is not recommended to use this option if
short compile time is important.
• It is not recommended to use -sysc=adjust_timeres option in combination with
partition compile flow, as it increases the elaboration time.
Do not use this option for SystemC-top designs in combination with partition
compile flow.
Adding a Main Routine for Verilog-On-Top Designs
Normally, a Verilog-on-top design does not contain a sc_main() function, as all SystemC
instantiations are performed within the Verilog modules. However, it is possible to add a
main routine to perform several initialization for the SystemC side.
The following are the basic steps to perform this function:
• Create a C++ source file which contains the main function (see the following example).
Do not name this main function as sc_main.
• Add the registration function which takes care of the proper calling of the user-defined
main routine.
• Analyze the file using syscan user_main.cpp . This adds the file to the design
database. Note that, there are no other options required to analyze this file.
The user-defined main routine must is similar to the following:
// File: user_main.cpp
int user_main_function(int argc, char **argv)
{
// you have access to the argc, argv arguments:
for (int i = 0; i < (argc-1); ++i)
std::cerr << Arg[" << i << "] = " << argv[i] << "\n";

extern "C" int sc_main_register(int (*)(int, char **));
static int my_sc_main = sc_main_register(user_main_function);

Support for AMS With SystemC Design
Verilog-AMS flow is supported in the following design topologies:
• A Verilog design that contains SystemC and Verilog/VHDL entities.
• A SystemC design that contains Verilog and VHDL entities.
• A VHDL design that contains SystemC leaf modules and Verilog/ VHDL entities.
Verilog-AMS flow is supported in all the design topologies with the -sysc=amsoption
when executing the VCS elaboration. This option specifies that the design contains AMS
instances with the SystemC designs.
This section provides the use model to support AMS with SystemC designs:
For each AMS instance, a corresponding Verilog or VHDL entity is required which is used
as a placeholder in the elaboration step.
During runtime, these instances are replaced with the AMS designs.
The configuration in AMS control file are available in the init file that is passed to the
elaborator step in the -ad=<file>.init control file. This init file contains the mappings
and the simulator that needs to be used for elaboration.
To activate the design with SystemC and AMS, the -sysc=ams option must be used when
executing the VCS elaboration. If the option is not used, then an error message appears
mentioning that AMS is not supported.
The following example illustrates usage of the -sysc=ams option:
• vcs -sysc -sysc=ams -sysc <TopLevel_ModuleName> -ad=sp.init

Compile Flow Limitations
Compile Flow Limitations
The following limitations apply to the VCS/SystemC interface:
• No donuts/sandwiches for SystemC-on-Top
VCS/SystemC does not support having "donuts" or "sandwiches" in the modules where
the top entity is SystemC.
• Number of ports
There is no limitation regarding the number of ports for an interface model. It may have
none, one, or multiple ports.
• You cannot compile mixed designs (SystemC+HDL) in a directory where the directory
path/name contains the symbol ‘:’. For instance, if you have a ‘:’ in your directory path/
name, as illustrated in the following, a compilation error can be triggered. Depending
on the complexity of your flow, an elaboration error can also be triggered.
/remote/vg/work/mixed_design:example/build/
• VCS/SystemC does not support wrapper creation for a templatized SystemC module.
Also, creation of a SystemC/HDL interface model and a TLI adapter is not supported
for a templatized SystemC module.
file aaa.h: template<int W> SC_MODULE(AAA) {…};
file aaa.cpp: #include "aaa.h"
syscan aaa.h:AAA // SC/HDL interface model -> error
syscan aaa.h -tli AAA.tli // TLI -> error
syscan aaa.cpp // just compile cpp file -> OK
• VCS-SystemC co-simulation interface does not support parallel VPD dumping.
• Verilog wrapper is needed for pure VHDL-top-SystemC down.
The topology with VHDL-on-top and SystemC-down is supported in the UUM flow, but
the following restriction is observed:
◦ A Verilog wrapper must be created for at least one SystemC interface model.
SystemC modules that are to be instantiated in VHDL entities are analyzed with
-vhdl option in the syscan call.
syscan -vhdl mymodel1.cpp:mymodel1
You can continue to use the -vhdl option for the majority of SystemC interface
models, however, at least one module that is used within the design must be
created without this option.

Compiling SystemC Designs in Partition Compile Flow
syscan -vhdl mymodel1.cpp:mymodel1
syscan -vhdl mymodel2.cpp:mymodel2
syscan mymodel3.cpp:mymodel3
vhdlan bottom.vhd top.vhd
vcs -sysc TOP
Note that the syscan call for mymodel3 has no "-vhdl" option, that is, a Verilog
wrapper is created.
• Recommended VCS version checks during Migration
◦ To avoid linking errors and crashes when moving from one release to another
during migration, compile all the files from the beginning.
When a design or shared library is compiled with a VCS SystemC version, a
reference symbol snps_vcs_sc_api_version_m_20XX_YY_scZZZ is inserted.
This symbol ensures that all the files, objects, or libraries of the design are compiled
with the same VCS version. For example, if the version is not the same everywhere
in a design complied with VCS-2023.03 for SystemC-2.3.4, then the following link
error is issued:
undefined reference to
`sc_core::snps_vcs_sc_api_version_u_2023_03_s
c234<&(sc_core::SC_DISABLE_VIRTUAL_BIND_UNDEF
INED_)>::snps_vcs_sc_api_version_u_2023_03_sc
234(sc_core::sc_writer_policy)'
where,
u_2023_03(respectively 234) is the VCS (respectively SystemC) version used.
Compiling SystemC Designs in Partition Compile Flow
You can compile the SystemC designs with VCS in the partition compile flow.
This section contains the following sub sections which provide more details about how to
use SystemC designs in the partition compile flow:
• SystemC Partition Compile Example
• Limitation

Compiling SystemC Designs in Partition Compile Flow
To compile the code shown in Example 2 in the partition compile flow, use the following
commands:
1. Analyze the Verilog child module:
% vlogan -sysc sc_model vlog_mod vlog_mod.v
2. Compile the SystemC module:
% syscan sc_mod.cpp sc_top.cpp
3. Analyze the configuration file:
% vlogan partcomp_cfg.v
4. Elaborate the design:
% vcs -sysc partcomp_cfg -partcomp \
-partcomp_dir="VCS_SYSC_LIB" -lca
Generally the top-level module name is specified to VCS in the
UUM
UUM flow.
Here, you must specify the configuration module name to VCS. In step 4, the
configuration module name is partcomp_cfg.
This feature has the following limitation:
• Partition Compile flow do not work with designs containing SystemC donut
configuration, that is, an HDL layer embedded within a SystemC layer, which in turn is
embedded in an HDL layer.
• When -sysc=opt_if or -sysc=dpi_if options are used, extra internal modules are
created. This might create problems with Partition Compile because compilation fails
with partcomp, and -sysc=opt_if.
For successful compilation, add the following line to the partcomp config file:default
liblist DEFAULT; .

Simulation Flow
This chapter describes different simulation/runtime options or flows for VCS SystemC co-
simulation and includes the following topics:
• Specifying Runtime Options to the SystemC Simulation
• Controlling Simulation From sc_main
• Enabling E115 Check in VCS Co-Simulation Interface
• Delta-Cycles
• Increasing Stack and Stack Guard Size
• Guidelines to Diagnose Stack Overrun
• Using POSIX Threads or Quickthreads
• Generating Profile Reports for SystemC Designs
• Viewing SystemC sc_report_handler Messages from Log File
• Debugging SystemC Simulation Errors
Specifying Runtime Options to the SystemC Simulation
You can start a simulation with the simv command line. The command line arguments can
be either passed to the VCS simulator only, or to the sc_main() function only or to both of
these.
By default, all command-line arguments are provided to sc_main(), and the VCS
simulator kernel. All arguments following -systemcrun are passed to sc_main(). All
arguments following -verilogrun are passed to the VCS simulator kernel. Arguments
specified before the first -systemcrun or -verilogrun usually are passed to both
sc_main(),and the VCS simulator kernel unless they are VCS-specific arguments such
as, -ucli or -gui.
For example:
simv -ucli a b -verilogrun c d -systemcrun e f g

Controlling Simulation From sc_main
The sc_main() function receives the "a b e f g " arguments and the VCS simulator
kernel receives the "-ucli a b c d " arguments.
Controlling Simulation From sc_main
VCS supports multiple calls to the
sc_start
sc_start() routine inside the
sc_main
sc_main() function. This
allows you to control the simulation from the sc_main() function and enables you to add
more functionality in sc_main() after a call to sc_start(). Sometimes you need to add a
functionality after a call to sc_start when you know that a particular condition for the end
of simulation is not met.
For SystemC-on-top and pure SystemC designs, you write the entry point function
sc_main() where the top-level SystemC modules are instantiated. The simulation starts
by calling sc_start() inside sc_main(). When you call the sc_start() routine with a
time argument, the simulation runs until the specified time and returns to sc_main(). This
allows you to control the simulation by taking appropriate actions at different simulation
times. This functionality is only available in the SystemC deltasync flow.
In previous releases, VCS started the simulation with a call to sc_start () and
kept running until the simulation terminated. Therefore, the control never came
back to the sc_main() function.
This feature removes the following restrictions on coding style inside sc_main() that were
required for the save/restore feature:
• The need to use dynamic allocation for
sc_objects
sc_objects inside sc_main()is not required.
However, it is recommended to use dynamic allocation to avoid stack overflow in the
sc_main thread.
• Multiple sc_start() calls are supported and statements located after sc_start() are
executed.
The sc_main() function is treated as a thread in VCS-SystemC co-
simulation.
The sc_main thread is run with the default stack size, which is usually 10 MB. At times,
the sc_main function may create several SystemC objects and hence consume a huge
amount of stack space.
The following three ways are provided to alter the stack size of the sc_main thread:
• Use the
-sysc=stacksize1024k
-sysc=stacksize:1024k runtime switch to set the stack size. This is the
same switch used to set the stack size for SC_THREADS. Since the sc_main thread
is usually heavier compared to SC_THREADS, VCS allocates 16 times to the value
specified with this switch.

Controlling Simulation From sc_main
• Use the
VCS_SYSC_STACKSIZE
setenv VCS_SYSC_STACKSIZE 1024k environment variable to set the stack
size. This is an alternative to the above switch. Here, VCS allocates 16 times to the
specified value. The runtime switch takes precedence over this environment setting.
• Use the following API call to set the stack size:
sc_snps::sc_set_stack_size_sc_main(const char* size_string)
You can call this API and specify the stack size as a string (for example, 1024 k ).
Call this routine before the sc_main() function gets called. You can perform this by
placing this function call in a static initializer outside the sc_main function. Note that
the systemc_user.h header file must be included since the sc_snps namespace is
declared in the header file.
static int tmp =
sc_snps::sc_set_stack_size_sc_main("1024K");
When you use any or all of the above methods to alter the stack size, the final size is the
maximum value of the following:
• The default size.
• Size set using runtime switch or environment variable.
• Size set using the API call.
Since VCS executes sc_main within a thread, you should use dynamic allocation for
sc_object created inside sc_main to minimize the stack utilization.
Following is the limitation of controlling simulation from sc_main:
The stack size cannot be modified for simulations that contain only SystemC not
no HDL code. Function sc_main runs in the main stack of simv. Runtime argument
-sysc=stacksize, the environment variable and calls to sc_set_stack_size_sc_main()
is silently ignored.
Setting the Return Code of simv
To exit a simulation with an exit status same as the value returned by sc_main, you can
use the following VCS API:
void VcsSetExitFunc(int (*)(int));

Controlling Simulation From sc_main
You can use this API to register a user-specified function with VCS. VCS calls the
registered user-specified function immediately after the simulation ends, where you can
end the simulation with the required exit codes.
//Inside the file containing sc_main function

#include "sc_top.h"

extern "C" void VcsSetExitFunc(int (*)(int));

/* global variable which will store the exit status */
int exit_code=0;

/* user specified function registered with VCS API */
int exit_handler(int flag)
{

Effect on end_of_simulation Callbacks
At the end of simulation, the SystemC kernel provides callbacks to a user-defined function
named end_of_simulation which can be defined in any SC_MODULE. This is possible only
if the entire SystemC design is present when the simulation ends.
SystemC simulation is terminated in the following cases:
• sc_stop() is called
• $finish is called on the Verilog side
• sc_main function returns
Two of the above conditions can be detected before the design gets cleaned up, but the
last condition cannot be detected before the design gets freed up. Once the sc_main
returns, all sc_objects that are statically allocated are deleted. Therefore, the SystemC
kernel cannot issue end_of_simulation callbacks on these deleted sc_objects.
Therefore, you must add an sc_stop() call at the end of the sc_main() function (before
returning from it). Example 3 shows a code snippet with multiple sc_start calls.
Example 3 Multiple sc_start Calls
int sc_main()
{

title: Verification Continuum™

sc_start(t); /* Execute till time t */

sc_start(t1); /* Execute till time t1 */

sc_stop(); /* Call end_of_simulation routines for
sc_modules */
}
Compile the design as follows:
% vcs -sysc -lca

For pure SystemC designs, whenever there are multiple drivers on the sc_signal, the
E115 error message Multiple DKI-drivers found gets triggered. For mixed SystemC-

Enabling E115 Check in VCS Co-Simulation Interface
HDL designs, whenever there are multiple drivers on sc_signal and at least one of
the drivers is from HDL, a warning message gets triggered by default. This helps you
to diagnose incorrect simulation results occurring due to the usage of wrong channel
type instead of sc_signal_rv or sc_signal_resolved channel in mixed SystemC-HDL
designs.
The following warning message is issued during simulation:
Warning-[SYSC-E115-W] Multiple DKI-drivers found
Multiple DKI-drivers found:
signal `sc_top.outputmult' (sc_signal) first driver
`sc_top.adder_inst.adder_outx_action'
(sc_method_process) second driver
`sc_top.subtracter_inst.subtracter_action'
(sc_method_process)
The signal is driven by both an HDL as well as an SystemC
source but values will not be properly resolved. Simulation
results may be incorrect.
We recommend to modify the design and use inout ports plus
option '-sysc=opt_if' for SC/HDL interface models to get
proper resolution for these multiple drivers.
Use runtime option
'-sysc=enable_multiple_dki_driver_check' to turn this
warning into an error. Use runtime option
'-sysc=disable_multiple_dki_driver_check' to turn off
this warning.
This warning can be disabled using any one of the following options:
• Using the runtime option:
-sysc=disable_multiple_dki_driver_check
• Using the C API inside sc_main() at the beginning, before the constructors are called:
int sc_main()
{
disable_multiple_dki_driver_check(1);

}
The warning can also be converted into an error using one of the following options:
• Using the runtime option:
-sysc=enable_multiple_dki_driver_check
• Using the environment variable:
% setenv SYSC_STRICT1666_DKI 2

Error:
Error-[SYSC-E115-E] Multiple DKI-drivers found
Multiple DKI-drivers found: signal `sc_top.outputmult'
(sc_signal) first driver `sc_top.multiplier_inst.port_2'
(sc_out) second driver `sc_top.subtracter_inst.xx'
(sc_out) The signal is driven by both an HDL as well as
an SystemC source but values will not be properly resolved.
Simulation results may be incorrect.
We recommend to modify the design and use inout ports plus
option '-sysc=opt_if' for SC/HDL interface models to get
proper resolution for these multiple drivers.
Use runtime option
'-sysc=disable_multiple_dki_driver_check' to turn off
this error.
VPD dumping of delta-cycles is supported for SystemC elements, but, it is disabled by
default. To enable this feature, perform the following steps:

text:
Using HDL and SystemC Sync Loops
VCS SystemC enables you to simulate both HDL (Verilog, SystemVerilog, VHDL) and
SystemC together. A sync loop drives the kernels of both HDL and SystemC parts and
ensures that simulation events stay aligned. There are two different sync-loops to select
from which differ in simulation speed, accuracy of the alignment, and other aspects.
The two sync loops are as follows:
• The coarse-grained sync loop (blocksync).
• The fine-grained sync loop (deltasync). This is default.
Coarse-Grained Sync Loop (blocksync)
This sync loop aligns HDL and SystemC at a coarse but efficient level. If there are multiple
delta cycles on the SystemC side, some or all of those SystemC delta cycles are executed
consecutively before control is handed back to the HDL side.
Similarly, multiple Verilog/VHDL delta cycles might happen before the next set of SystemC
delta cycles are started. This schema is efficient in terms of simulation time. However, the
interaction between HDL and SystemC is difficult to predict.
This is done by specifying the -sysc=blocksync argument during elaboration. For
example,
vcs -sysc -sysc=blocksync
Fine-Grained Sync Loop (deltasync)
If fine-grained and easy-to-predict alignment between HDL and SystemC is preferred, then
use the fine-grained SC/HDL sync loop.
Run Time
The simulation speed might be affected by using the fine-grained sync loop. The difference
depends on the individual design, therefore there is no simple rule-of-thumb. However,
there is a general tendency that simulations run slower when using the fine-grained sync
loop.

Alignment of Delta Cycles
In the fine-grained SC/HDL sync loop, delta cycles of SystemC and Verilog are aligned. If
at a specific simulation time, there are both SystemC and Verilog events present that span
over multiple delta cycles each, then execution of events is aligned as follows:
1. Handle SystemC and Verilog events:
◦ If SystemC events are present at current simulation time:
Execute one SystemC delta cycle.
◦ If Verilog events are present at current simulation time:
Execute all Verilog events at the current simulation time until there are only NBAs
left.
2. Update all SystemC signals, execute all Verilog NBAs, and exchange all value updates
between SystemC and Verilog.
The steps repeat until there are no more events at the current time, then proceed to the
next simulation time. That is, SystemC delta cycles and Verilog NBAs are strictly aligned.
The order in which the step 1 operations are executed is not specified. However, step

chapter: 2 happens only after both step 1 operations are completed. The order should not effect
title: 2 happens only after both step 1 operations are completed. The order should not effect
text:
because value updates are only performed after both sides have finished their delta
cycle. If there are no SystemC events in a specific delta cycle, then the SystemC event
operation in step 1 is skipped. If there are no existing Verilog events, then the Verilog
event operation in step 1 is skipped.
Example Syntax
vlogan verilog_dut.v verilog_top.v

syscan ./stimulus.cpp:stimulus ./gen_clk.cpp:gen_clk -cflags "-g"

vcs top -debug_access+all -cflags "-g"
simv -ucli -i dump.tcl
Restrictions
The following restriction applies to the fine-grained SC/HDL sync loop:
• The time resolution between SystemC and HDL must match. An error is issued and the
simulation is stopped during startup of simv, when this restriction is violated.

Benefits of the deltasync Loop
The deltasync loop offers the following benefits compared to the blocksync loop:
• Clear scheduling semantics.
If your design is sensitive to ordering of SystemC delta cycles within the same time
step and to the interactions between SystemC and HDL, then the deltasync loop
provides better predictability regarding when and how value updates between SC and
HDL are propagated.
• The VCS slave mode in combination with SystemC is only available with the
deltasync loop.
• The process save/restore feature in combination with SystemC is only available with
the deltasync loop.
Simulation Differences Between blocksync and deltasync Loop
It is possible that an existing design containing SystemC simulates differently with
blocksync and deltasyncloop. This section describes possible scenarios of difference
between blocksync and deltasyncloops and offers explanations or solutions.
Scenario 1 - Mismatched Time Resolution
If SystemC and HDL parts contain different time resolutions, the deltasync loop
terminates the simulation with the following error message:
Error-[SC-TRES-E] Time resolution mismatch
The time resolution of SystemC is set to 1ps but Verilog is
set to 1s. Please adjust time resolution with option
'-sysc=adjust_timeres' during elaboration or use statements
like '`timescale 100ps / 10ps' in Verilog or
'sc_set_time_resolution(10, SC_PS);' in SystemC.
This message contains the actual settings within the design (printed in bold, 1ps versus
1s). You can use these values to adjust either the SystemC or the HDL side.
If you encounter this error, then you need to adjust the time resolutions in one of the
following ways:
• Elaborate with the -timescale=… option. If the resolution on the HDL side is not
defined by any other means, then adjust it to the SystemC value, which you find in the
first line of the error message. In the earlier mentioned example, it is 1ps, therefore,
elaborate again with vcs … -timescale=1ns/1ps …

• Elaborate with the -sysc=adjust_timeresoption. This option tries to automatically
adjust the time resolution on either SystemC or HDL side. Note that, this is not possible
in all cases and that the option increases the compile time.
• Set the resolution on the SystemC side with a
'sc_set_time_resolution(10,SC_PS)' statement in your SystemC source code.
See the section “Controlling TimeScale and Resolution” for a detailed description of these
approaches.
The blocksync loop issues a warning instead of an error and continues the
simulation. Here, the simulation is slower and might show incorrect results or
might even hang due to mismatched time resolution. Therefore, it is always
better to adjust the time resolutions as mentioned in this section.
Scenario 2 - Differences During Initialization Phase of the Simulation
When the simulation starts, both SystemC and HDL domains process initial events.
For example, the SystemC domain processes the SC_METHOD processes that have no
dont_initialize() statement. The HDL domain processes Verilog initial statements.
VCS executes such initial events from both domains during simulation startup.
The order with respect to how SystemC and HDL initial events are aligned might be
different between blocksync and deltasync. For example, some statements are issued
in a different order. It is also possible that the design gives different simulation results after
the init phase due to these changes.
For example, consider the case of the following two initial events:
Verilog: initial AA= 10;
and
SystemC SC_METHOD executing BB = AA
Both are executed as initial events. The value of BB depends on the order in which they
are executed and might be 10 or 0.
Another example is a SystemC sc_clock signal that has a posedge at t=0. This is read in
the HDL domain also at t=0. The HDL side might view transitions from X01 or just X1
during the init phase.
Its recommended to make such designs robust by using a reset signal that is active at
t=0. This remains active for a short time after t=0. Alternatively, you can wait with event
processing in testbenches and so on until t>0.
Scenario 3 - Race Conditions Between Delta Cycles and Domains

The change in alignment of delta-cycles and NBA events might expose a race condition
in the design. This might lead to different simulation results or hanging simulations. This is
not a bug of the deltasync loop but a race condition in the design.
Consider a case where a SystemC testbench produces a value change on signal AA that
propagates within SystemC causing signal BB to change. The value change of AA is also
propagated into the HDL domain where it leads to Verilog signal CC changing. This is sent
back to SystemC. All these changes happen within the same time step but in different
delta cycles/NBA queues. Now, assume a SystemC process that is sensitive to value
change of AA, BB, and CC. It looks at the values of BB and CC to decide what to do. If
BB changes before CC, then it proceeds one way. If they change simultaneously, then it
behaves in another way.
This design has a race condition with the combined event ordering of SystemC and HDL.
The design might simulate differently because the deltasync loop is default.
With the blocksync loop, the value change of BB probably arrives before the one from
CC. Because entire clusters of SystemC delta cycles are executed before HDL events
are processed. The value change thus propagates faster inside the SystemC domain
than across SystemCHDLSystemC. However, with deltasync, delta-cycles, and NBA
updates are aligned, value change propagate equally fast through SystemC and through
Verilog NBAs.
On comparing blocksync and deltasync loops, the SystemC process looking at both BB
and CC views different values. The simulation might fail to work in the same way as before
with blocksync.
You can restore the previous behavior by adding -sysc=blocksyncelaboration option.
However, the benefits of the deltasync loop mentioned earlier are missed and the race
condition remains in the design. Alternatively, you can identify and fix the race condition.
Scenario 4 - Differences When the Simulation Ends
The simulation ends when $finish is called on the Verilog side or sc_stop() is called on
the SystemC side. In these situations, you might notice a difference between blocksync
and deltasync loop.
There might still be events on either side, ready to be executed after $finish/sc_stop
is called. The number of these events that are still executed before the simulation actually
shuts down can differ between blocksync and deltasync loop.
Scenario 5 - Different Execution Order of Concurrent Delta Cycles / NBA Queues
The SystemC delta cycles and Verilog NBA queue events interleaving is different from
blocksync and deltasync loop. This can lead to differences in the simulation behavior,
for example, the order of output lines change.

Increasing Stack and Stack Guard Size
Such differences are possible if both domains have events ready to be executed that are
independent of each other. They run concurrently. In general, with concurrent events, no
specific order of execution is guaranteed.
The following is the limitation of the feature deltasync Loop:
When you use the deltasync loop, calling sc_start() with SC_EXIT_ON_STARVATION is
not supported. The sc_start() function might return too early or too late. Functions such
as sc_pending_activity() might not give the correct result. In these cases, the warning
message SC-START-STARVATION is reported.
To avoid this, elaborate your design with the -sysc=blocksync option. This method
avoids making multiple calls to sc_start() function.

SC_THREAD,
SC_CTHREAD
SC_CTHREAD,
sc_main, and spawned function or method). Since this stack is limited in size, you need to
choose an appropriate stack size.

segmentation violation
segmentation violation (

SEGV occurred in file1.cpp line 123

see the SystemC LRM.

quickthreads. Switching from one SC_THREAD to another is significantly slower with
pthreads than with quickthreads. However, pthreads have advantages in terms of
debugging support with gdb or Verdi/CBug or tools such as Purify or Valgrind.
If pthreads or quickthreads must be used depends on the platform which you can influence
in some case(s).
The following API allows you to select or check if pthreads are used (if supported on the
platform):
// Wish for either pthreads or quickthreads, return true
// if wish is granted, return false+produce warning if not
// possible.

bool sc_snps::request_to_use_pthreads(bool use_pthreads);

// use pthreads (true) or quickthreads for SC_[C]THREADS

bool sc_snps::use_pthreads();
The request_to_use_pthreads() function must be called before the simulation starts to
run for the first time, for example, before the first call of sc_start(). A good position in
which to place the statement is at the beginning of the simulation from a static initializer
call.
The function returns true if the request was granted. It returns false, if this is not possible
and also a warning message is issued. The reasons may be, wrong platform (for example,
RHEL32), or calling the function too late.

To enable using pthreads, you can also set the SYSC_USE_PTHREADS environment variable
to ‘1’ before running the simulator.
Generating Profile Reports for SystemC Designs
VCS enables you to generate profiling reports for SystemC designs which provide granular
detail of the time taken by your SystemC design during simulation.
This section outlines the support for profiling and the use model in the following sections:
• Time Profiling
• Memory Profiling
• SystemC Constructs Supported by simprofile
• Limitation
Time Profiling
Time profiling for SystemC is supported with the VCS
–simprofile
-simprofile option. CPU time
consumed by the SystemC model is listed in the overall profile report. This section
describes how to create the profile, what kind of data is reported, and its limitations.
Enabling Time Profiling at Compile-Time
Use the
–simprofile
-simprofile compile-time option on the VCS elaboration command line.
% vcs -simprofile <other_VCS_options>
Using Time Profiling at Runtime
When you run simv, VCS generates a profile report. To view the report in text format, use
the following command:
% profrpt -view time_all -format text -filter 0 \
simprofile_dir
The following different views are available in text format inside the profileReport directory:
1. TimeConstructView.txt — This is the construct view. It provides the time consumed
by constructs, along with the modules that own the constructs. The main constructs
for SystemC are SC processes, which can be
SC_METHODS
SC_METHODS,
SC_THREADS
SC_THREADS, or
SC_CTHREADS
SC_CTHREADS.
2. TimeModuleView.txt — This is the module view. It provides details about all
constructs in that particular module. If a module bot has two processes and is
instantiated three times, there should be six processes for module bot in this view.

Generating Profile Reports for SystemC Designs
3. TimeInstanceView.txt — This is the instance view. It provides the hierarchical path
name of the instance and the total inclusive and exclusive time for that instance. This
view also displays the module corresponding to the module instance.
4. TimeSC-Spawn-OverHeadView.txt – This view provides the total time spent in
SystemC overhead. The three main categories are as follows:
◦ SC-Value-OverHead — Shows the time spent in value exchanges between HDL
and SystemC and vice-versa.
◦ SC-Kernel-OverHead — Shows the time spent synchronizing between HDL and
SystemC, VPD dumping, and so on.
◦ SC-Spawn-OverHead — Shows overhead relating to all the spawned processes
(dynamic processes created with the sc_spawn() feature) in the entire SystemC
design.
5. TimeSummaryView.txt — This is the summary view. It provides the following two

Debugging SystemC Kernel Errors
VCS provides an effective mechanism to debug your design issues during elaboration and
runtime. You can use the cbug_stop_here() function that is called whenever a SystemC
kernel error occurs. You can use this function to place a breakpoint in this function and

view the stack trace to know the source code that is causing the error. The following
sections describe how you can troubleshoot your elaboration and runtime issues:
• Troubleshooting Elaboration Errors
• Troubleshooting Simulation Errors
• Function cbug_stop_here()
• Limitations
Troubleshooting Elaboration Errors
In SystemC-on-top designs, during elaboration, all SystemC constructors,
end_of_elaboration() methods and other statements (before sc_start) in sc_main
function are executed. It is possible that something goes wrong in these parts of source
code.
Whenever there is a SystemC kernel error during elaboration, VCS generates an
executable file simv.elab.error. This can be used for debugging the elaboration error
with gdb, as you can know which part of your source code is causing the elaboration error.
Consider a scenario where a SC-top design calls wait() within the sc_main() function.
This is not allowed by the SystemC language, so, a SC kernel error occurs. This in turn
breaks the entire elaboration and results in SC-VCS-SYSC-ELAB error. This is illustrated in
the following example.
% vlogan dut.v -sc_model dut
% syscan main.cpp -cflags -g
% vcs -sysc sc_main

SC_METHODs use next_trigger() instead

The design could not be fully elaborated due to an early termination of
the SystemC part of the design.
Please read the hints in file simv.elab.error.README or review the
details in the SystemC chapter of the VCS documentation.
The simv is not generated because the elaboration failed. However, an executable
file simv.elab.error gets generated that can be used for debugging and a test file
simv.README is also generated which provides hints on how to debug the failure.

Troubleshooting Simulation Errors
Whenever a SystemC kernel error occurs that terminates the simulation, you can use
the cbug_stop_here() function to debug such an issue. You must stop the simulation
inside the cbug_stop_here() function and look at the stack to find out which source code

Function cbug_stop_here()
Whenever a SystemC kernel error occurs that may terminate the simulation, VCS calls the
cbug_stop_here() function which is useful for debugging. It helps you to find out which
source code statement is triggering the error.
The cbug_stop_here() function has the following two arguments.
• The reason argument explains why the function is called, usually an error that
terminates the simulation shortly.
• The details argument provides additional information in some cases or might
be empty. The callstack provides more information and reveals the statement that
triggered the error in most cases.
This function is only available when SystemC is part of the simulation. It cannot be used,
for example, for a simulation that has Verilog and DPI but no SystemC.
The cbug_stop_here() function stops in the following situations:
• Argument reason=”P: sc_stop() called”:
If the sc_stop() function is called either from your SC source code or the SC kernel,
the simulation ends. Depending on the SystemC version and settings, it might stop
instantly or finish other SystemC and HDL processes also scheduled in the current
delta cycle.
• Argument reason=”Stop: SC_STOP in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and is about to call the SC_STOP action.
• Argument reason="Interrupt: SC_INTERRUPT in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and calls the SC_INTERRUPT action. The simulation
may continue or end depending on other actions from this sc_report.
• Argument reason=”Abort: SC_ABORT in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and calls the SC_ABORT action. The simulation ends
instantly.

• Argument reason=”Throw: sc_report is about to be thrown ”:
If sc_report is being processed and issues an sc_report object. The simulation ends
soon in most cases, however, it may also continue in the following case:
If there is a 'catch' statement in the surrounding source code, then it might take care
of sc_report and the simulation continues. However, if the exception is not caught in
your source code, then SC or VCS kernel catches it and terminates the simulation. If
so, then cbug_stop_here() is called again with reason 'Error from SC kernel '.
• Argument reason=”Error from SC kernel: sc_report was not caught and
terminates simulation ”:
If sc_report was thrown and not caught, the simulation ends. This is typically the
case when SC_REPORT_ERROR was called. Look in argument 'details' for the error
message.
• Argument reason="C++ exception was not caught and terminates
simulation":
If some kind of C++ exception was thrown and not caught in code, the simulation ends.
If the function is reached multiple times during a simulation and you want to stop only
at a specific call, then you must use a local variable no and a condition breakpoint. The
variable is incremented with each call.
There is a case statement inside the function with a case for each reason. You can use it
to set a breakpoint to a specific reason.
Note that the exact wording of the string inside “reason" is subject to change between
the VCS releases. The signature (the set of arguments) might also change between VCS
releases.
Debugging capabilities are very limited when the virtualizer flow (-sysc=snps_vp) is
used. The cbug_stop_here() function still exists, but is called only in a few cases. Most
SystemC kernel errors do not call cbug_stop_here().
Diagnosing Quickthread Issues
VCS is equipped with a better mechanism to report VCS runtime crashes caused by
certain problems with quickthreads used during VCS runtime. VCS provides feedback
regarding as to what went wrong and which thread is causing the crash, thereby enabling
you to take specific action to circumvent the issue. For more information on this feature,
see section Guidelines to Diagnose Stack Overrun and section “Diagnosing Quickthread
Issues in SystemC”in VCS User Guide.

Valgrind Usage for SystemC
VCS-SystemC simulation (simv) contains the user C++ code. This code may contain
some bugs leading to crashes or odd behavior. These types of bugs are usually tricky to
analyze, and tools like Valgrind may help quite a lot.
A typical Valgrind command line can look like this:
valgrind --tool=memcheck --num-callers=30 --trace-children=yes ./simv
-simv_arg …
Now the Valgrind usage on a VCS-SystemC simulation is significantly simplified.
The use model is just simv -valgrind with no extra setup.
Valgrind must be available on the machine where simv is executed. When simv
-valgrind is invoked, Valgrind executable is searched automatically from the VG GNU
package.
The simv -valgrind option calls Valgrind as follows:
valgrind --tool=memcheck --num-callers=30
--max-stackframe=600000000 --trace-children=yes
--trace-children-skip=/bin/*,/usr/local/bin/*,/usr/bin/*,/lib64/ld-linux
-x86-64.so.2,/usr/bin//*,$VCS_HOME/* ./simv …
Extra Valgrind options can be passed with the -valgrindopt option. The -valgrindopt
option can be used multiple times.
The following is an example:

m_state++;
if (m_state > 42) m_state = 0;
if (sc_time_stamp() > sc_time(0,SC_NS)) { outx.write(m_state);
// intentional error to be reported by Valgrind
int a;
std::cout << "a = " << a << "\n"; }
}

The usage model to simulate a design having a Verilog testbench with SystemC and
Verilog/VHDL instances involves the following steps:

For additional information, see Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for SystemC
Modules.
% vlogan [vlogan_options] file1.v file2.v
% vhdlan [vhdlan_options] file1.vhd file2.vhd

• Compilation
% vcs -sysc [compile_options] top_module
% simv [ runtime_options]
Input Files Required
To run co-simulation with a Verilog design containing SystemC instances, the following
input files are required:
• SystemC Source Code
◦ You can directly write the entity-under-test source code or generate it with other
tools.
◦ Any other C or C++ code for the design.
• Verilog or VHDL Source Code ( .v, .vhd, .vhdl extensions) including,
◦ Verilog wrapper for your SystemC module (see Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers
for SystemC Modules).
◦ Any other Verilog or VHDL source files for the design.
• An optional port mapping file
If you do not provide this file, the interface uses the default port mapping definition. For
details of the port mapping file, see Using Port Mapping File.

• An optional data type mapping file
If you do not write a data type mapping file, the interface uses the default mapping file
in the VCS installation. For details of the data type mapping files, see Using Data Type
Mapping File.
Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules
The
syscan utility
syscan utility is used to generate the wrapper and interface files for co-simulation.
This utility adds the sysc directory to the csrc directory in the current directory. The
syscan utility writes the wrapper and interface files in the subdirectories in the ./csrc/
sysc directory.
The syntax for the syscan command line is as follows:
%syscan [options] filename[:modulename] [filename[:modulename]]*
Where:
[options] can be any of the following:
-cc <path to compiler>
Displays the path to C compiler.
-cflags "flags"
Passes flags to the C++ compiler.
-cmp
Creates and compiles helpers.
-cpp path_to_the_compiler
Specifies the location of the C++ compiler. If you do not specify this option, VCS uses the
GNU g++ compiler, by default.
See the VCS Release Notes for details on all supported compiler versions.
debug_access+all
Prepares SystemC source files for interactive debugging.
-export_DPI <dpi-function>
Marks the dpi-function for SystemC.
-export_DPI <vlog-file>

Marks all export DPI tasks in the file for SystemC.
-f filename
Specifies a file containing one or more filename[:modulename] entries, as these entries
were on the command line.
-full64
Enables compilation and simulation in 64-bit mode.
-gen_only
Creates helpers but does not compile them (default).
-help|-h
Displays the syntax, options, and examples of the syscan command.
-help -tli
Displays help about TLI.
-idf <idf_file>
Creates transaction level interface helpers from the given interface definition file.
-l
Captures the syscan command and the output of the syscan command into the log file. It
creates a new file if the log does not exist. If a log already exists, which is not created by
the syscan command, it overwrites the existing content. If a log created by syscan already
exists, then the log file is appended with the existing content.
After creating simv using VCS, you may come across some extra content
captured in the syscan log file other than what was captured during a syscan
call. This is because the VCS command internally calls the syscan command.
-Mdir=directory_path
Specifies an alternate directory for csrc.
-o name
The syscan utility uses the specified name instead of the module name as the name of the
model.
Do not enter this option when you have multiple modules on the command line. Doing this,
displays an error condition.
-port port_mapping_file

Specifies a port mapping file. See Using Port Mapping File.
-prec[=<path>]
Enables usage of pre-compiled SystemC header files.
-q
Suppresses all the notes, messages, and warnings (or anything with a lesser severity than
‘ERROR’), appearing in the BMI messages generated by syscan or from tools called by
syscan.
Warnings created by gcc or gmake are not suppressed.
-sysc=<systemc-version>
Uses this SystemC version. Valid versions are: 233, 234 and 301.
-sysc=dpi_if
Uses DPI instead of PLI for value between SystemC and Verilog. Updates through DPI are
generally faster than PLI. The default value is PLI.
-sysc=nodpi_if
Uses PLI instead of DPI for value updates.
Generates optimized interface code.
-sysc=pli_if
Uses PLI interfaces for value updates.
-sysc=snps_vp
Uses this Virtualizer/SNPS_VP SystemC version.
-tli <tli_file>
Creates helpers but does not compile them.
-tli_D <source_file>
Creates direct member access code for all the sc-modules found in the specified source
file, but does not compile them.
-tli_gen_struct <source> -class <class_name> [-o <outputfile>]
Converts a SV class into a C++ struct.

-tlm2
Adds include directives for header files of the TLM 2.0.1 installation (located at
$VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/tlm) to the compiler call. These include directories have
precedence over other include directories specified with syscan -cflags "-I/my/tlm2/
include".
You do not specify the data type mapping file on the command line. For detailed
information, see Using Data Type Mapping File.
-tlm2=<dir>
Same as -tlm2option, but uses TLM installation from <dir>. Note that the definition of the
TLM generic payload class tlm::tlm_generic_payload inside <dir> must be identical
(same binary layout) as the OSCI TLM class shipped with VCS. If the option is used, then
VCS does not automatically add the TLI-3 (libsysctli.a) and VMM-SC (libvmmsc.a) libraries
to the link line. Contact your field representative in case you want to use either TLI-3 or
VMM-SC in combination with your own TLM2 installation.
-vhdl
Prepares all SystemC interface models specified for the VHDL domain.
-v
Displays the version number.
-V -V
Produces even more verbose messages.
-V
Displays code generation and build details. Use this option if you encounter errors, or are
interested in the flow that builds the design.
-vmmsc
Adds VMM-SC header files when invoking compiler, also includes TLM 2.0 header files.
-verilog |-vhdl
Generates wrapper for the specified language. -verilog is the default.
-w[work] <library>
Maps a design library name to the logical library name WORK, which receives the output
of the analyzer.
filename[:modulename] [filename[:modulename]]*

Specifies all the SystemC files in the design. There is no limit to the number of files.
You must include :modulename for those SystemC modules that are directly instantiated
in your Verilog/VHDL design. Consider an example where the testbench instantiates
three SystemC modules at the same hierarchy level namely mod1(filename-mod1.cpp/
mod1.h), mod2(filename-mod2.cpp/mod2.h), and mod3(mod3.cpp/mod3.h).SystemC
module mod1 further instantiates the following two SystemC modules:
• dummy1(filename-dummy1.cpp/dummy1.h)
• dummy2(filename-dummy2.cpp/dummy2.h)
In this case, you can generate the wrapper using the following command:
% syscan mod1.cpp:mod1 mod2.cpp:mod2 mod3.cpp:mod3
For all SystemC modules that are not instantiated inside your Verilog/VHDL design,
:modulename can be omitted. You can compile SystemC modules dummy1 and dummy2 that
were instantiated under SystemC module mod1 using the following syscan command:
% syscan dummy1.cpp dummy2.cpp
The .cpp files are compiled and added to the design’s database, so that the final vcs
command is able to bring together all the modules in the design. You need not add -I
$VCS_HOME/include or -I$SYSTEMC/include.
The following example generates a Verilog wrapper:
syscan -cflags "-g" sc_add.h:sc_ad
Creating Verilog/VHDL Wrapper from SystemC Header File
You can create a Verilog/VHDL wrapper from a SystemC header file containing a SystemC
module. You can specify a different module name, a different header file name and a
different source file name altogether.
Compilation Steps:
% syscan my_file.h:my_mod
% syscan my_modc.cpp
Where, the SystemC module my_mod is defined in my_file.h. The corresponding source
file my_modc.cpp must be compiled separately.
The header file must be self-contained. The SystemC header file and the
corresponding cpp source file must be compiled with syscan using the same
pre-processor defines. If -Mdir option is used, then you must ensure that the
header file and the corresponding cpp files are compiled into the same Mdir
library. Otherwise, it gives elaboration errors.

% syscan my_file.h:my_mod -cflags "-DMY_DEF=1 -UUNDEF_ME"
% syscan my_file.cpp -cflags "-DMY_DEF=1 -UUNDEF_ME"
Where, the first syscan call creates only an interface for the SystemC module my_mod by
explicitly defining MY_DEF, and un-defining UNDEF_ME. The second call to syscan compiles
the implementation (and more) of the interface module. Here, the same defines and
undefines are used.
Supported Port Data Types
SystemC types are restricted to sc_clock, sc_bv, sc_logic, sc_lv, sc_int, sc_uint,
sc_bigint, and sc_biguint data types.
Native C/C++ types are restricted to uint, uchar, ushort, int, bool, short, char, long,
longlong, ulong, and ulonglongtypes.
Verilog ports are restricted to bit, bit-vector and signed bit-vector types.
VHDL ports are restricted to bit, bit-vector, standard logic, standard logic vector ,
signed and unsigned types.
In-out ports that cross the co-simulation boundary between SystemC and Verilog must
observe the following restrictions:
• SystemC port types must be sc_inout_rv<> or sc_inout_resolved and must be
connected to signals of type sc_signal_rv<> or sc_signal_resolved.
• Verilog port types must be bit_vector or bit.
• VHDL port types must be std_logic_vector or std_logic.
• You need to create a port mapping file, as described in Using Port Mapping File, to
specify the SystemC port data types as sc_lv (for a vector port) or sc_logic (for a
scalar port).
In SystemC ports of type structure, class or union are not supported.
In this example, you have a Verilog testbench, a SystemC module, stimulus, Verilog
module, display, and a VHDL entity, fir.
// SYSTEMC MODULE: stimulus
#include "stimulus.h"

void stimulus::entry()
{
cycle++;
// sending some reset values
if (cycle<25)
{
reset.write(SC_LOGIC_1);
input_valid.write(SC_LOGIC_0);
}
else
{
reset.write(SC_LOGIC_0);
input_valid.write( SC_LOGIC_0 );
