DWARF Based SystemC Front-End
Debugging With Arbitrary Record Formats (DWARF) is a file format for debugging
information that is commonly used in UNIX-like systems. The SystemC front-end, which is
DWARF based type API is the default interface. This front-end can be used in the creation
of SystemC-down interface models and in TLI direct-access flow. The front-end provides
support for C++11 constructs. It extracts port signature information from the user-compiled
binaries with debug capabilities such as, .o and *.so object files. This is, even if header
and source files are not available. This functionality is not available with Edison Design
Group (EDG) SystemC/C++ front-end.
Extracting the port signature while creating SystemC-down interface models is the only
step that is changed when compared to the SystemC/HDL interface model creation.
This front-end reads DWARF information. This provides a high-level API to access
information about C++ class/struct and other types. The relevant user C++ file is compiled
with the debug information. Then the interface extracts the port signature and other
necessary information. Object code with debug information is a prerequisite with this
interface. However, it is not necessary for Edison Design Group (EDG) SystemC/C++
front-end.
You can create a wrapper for SystemC/HDL interface models from object files (such as, .o
and *.so) that are created by the source files using the g++ call and compiled with the -g
debug switch, even if header and source files are not available with you. The .o and .so
files must be provided.
Following are the examples that illustrate the use model for creating Verilog interface
model for sc_top SystemC module for .o and .so files:
• .o files
g++ -I. -I${PWD}/csrc/sysc/include -I${VCS_HOME}/
include/systemc233 -Iinclude -I${VCS_HOME}/lib -
I${VCS_HOME}/include -I${VCS_HOME}/include/cosim/bf -I/
include -I. -g -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -MMD -m32 -fPIC -c
sc_top.cpp -o sc_top.o
syscan -cpp g++ sc_top.o:sc_top
• .so files

g++ -I. -I${PWD}/csrc/sysc/include -I${VCS_HOME}/
include/systemc233 -Iinclude -I${VCS_HOME}/lib -
I${VCS_HOME}/include -I${VCS_HOME}/include/cosim/bf -I/
include -I. -g -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -MMD -m32 -fPIC -c
sc_top.cpp -o sc_top.o
g++ -g -fPIC -shared -o sc_top.so sc_top.o -m32
(if you have 64-bit architecture, then use -m64 instead
of -m32)
syscan -cpp g++ sc_top.so:sc_top
Points to Note
• An archive file, *.a, cannot be used as input. This is, because an ar archive file is
not in the ELF format and DWARF requires ELF file type.
• In a regular syscan flow, there is an additional g++ call that compiles the SystemC/ C+
+ header or input source files with debug information. This, then uses this interface to
extract the port signature and other information. The compilation occurs internally. It is
not required to do any changes/modifications.
• If the module name is not specified in the syscan call, specify one or multiple module
names in the syscan call. Use the -sc_module option to generate the corresponding
code.
For example, following is the use model to create interface model for an SC module
called BusModel:
syscan -tli_DA -sc_model BusModel -sc_model BusModel2 -sc_model
BusModel3+BusModel4 BusModel.cpp

syscan -cflags "-g" -tlm2 BusModel.cpp:BusModel
Were, interface models are created for BusModel, BusModel2, BusModel3, and
BusModel4 SystemC modules.
• Use the _SNPS_SCFE_ predefined macro in this front-end to enable or disable SystemC
front-end parsing of certain pieces of code.
SystemC/C++ unused variables might not be visible in GUI because of GCC optimizations.
Compiling Interface Models with acc_user.h and vhpi_user.h
The header file, acc_user.h is provided by VCS and contains many #define macros and
type definitions. Some of these definitions, for example '#define bool int', may conflict
with C++ class definitions in user code. Similarly, header file vhpi_user.h is also provided
by VCS and may also conflict with C++ class definitions in user code.

SystemC/HDL interface models require to make at least some of these definitions visible
to compile the internal interface code. The amount of definitions can be controlled when
syscan is called. Three use models are available as follows:
Use Model 1
Only a minimal subset of definitions from acc_user.hand vhpi_user.h are made visible.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=0
Chances for a clash of those definitions with user C++ classes are minimal. Note that it is
neither possible to include acc_user.h nor vhpi_user.h in the user C++ source code.
Use Model 2
All definitions from acc_user.h (and vhpi_user.h if a VHDL interface is created) are
made visible, except the following macros: ("#define") : bool, true, TRUE, false, FALSE,
global, exfunc, local, null.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=1
The user code can include header files acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h, where the macros
mentioned earlier are #undef'ed in some situations.
The user code must include bf_user.h before including acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h file.
#include "bf_user.h"
#include "acc_user.h"
Use Model 3
All definitions from acc_user.h (and vhpi_user.h if a VHDL interface is created) are
made visible. Only macro "bool" is not visible.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags
or
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=2

The user code can include header files acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h, all
definitions including the macros mentioned above are visible.

Refer to “Adding a Main Routine for Verilog-On-Top Designs” to view the steps
to add a main routine to perform several initialization for the SystemC side.
Bind Limitations
The SystemVerilog “bind” statement does not support binding an SVA construct to a
SystemC instance.
The instantiation of the SystemC module must be a direct instantiation in the Verilog
module similar to instantiating any other Verilog module.
To co-simulate a SystemC design that contains Verilog and VHDL modules, you need
to create header files for those Verilog/ VHDL instances which directly interact with the
SystemC design. The header files is named as module_name.h for Verilog modules, and
entity_name.h for VHDL designs (see Example ). You can analyze other Verilog and
VHDL files using the vlogan, vhdlan executables. The ports of the created SystemC
wrapper are connected to signals that are attached to the ports of the corresponding
Verilog/ VHDL modules.

Input Files Required
To run co-simulation with a SystemC design containing Verilog and VHDL modules, the
following input files are required:
• Verilog and VHDL source code ( .v, .vhd, and .vhdl extensions)
◦ Verilog/ VHDL source files necessary for the design.
• SystemC source code including,
◦ A SystemC top-level simulation ( sc_main) that instantiates the interface wrappers
and other SystemC modules.
◦ Any other SystemC source files for the design.
• An optional port mapping file.
If you do not provide this file, the interface uses the default port mapping definition. For
details of the port mapping file, see Using Port Mapping File.

• An optional data type mapping file.
If you do not write a data type mapping file, the interface uses the default file in the

Generating SystemC Wrapper for Verilog Modules
Use the
vlogan utility
vlogan utility with the -sc_model option to generate and build the wrapper and
interface files for Verilog modules for co-simulation. This utility creates the ./csrc/sysc
directory in the current directory. The vlogan utility writes the header and interface files in
the ./csrc/sysc/include directory.
The syntax for the vlogan command line:
vlogan [options]-sc_model modulename file.v
Here, the following options can be used:
-sc_model modulename file.v
Specifies the module name and its Verilog source file.
-cpp path_to_the_compiler
Specifies the location of the C compiler. If you omit -cpp path , your environment uses the
GNU g++ compiler by default.
• See the VCS Release Notes for more details on supported compiler
versions.
• You can override the default compilers in your environment by supplying a
path to the g++ compiler. For example,
-cpp /usr/bin/g++
-sc_portmap port_mapping_file
Specifies a port mapping file. For additional information, see Using Port Mapping File.
-Mdir=directory_path
Works the same way that the -Mdir VCS compile-time option works. If you are using
the -Mdir option with VCS, you should use the -Mdir option with vlogan to redirect the
vlogan output to the same location that VCS uses.
-V

Displays code generation and build details. Use this option if you are encountering errors
or are interested in the flow that builds the design.
For example, the following command line generates a SystemC wrapper and interface file
for a Verilog module display:
vlogan -sc_model display display.v
Generating SystemC Wrapper for VHDL Designs
The vhdlan -sc_model utility can be used to generate and build the wrapper and
interface files for VHDL modules for co-simulation. This utility creates the ./csrc/sysc
directory in the current directory. The vhdlan utility writes the header and interface files in
the subdirectories in the ./csrc/sysc/include directory.
The following is the syntax for the vhdlan command line:
vhdlan [options]-sc_model entity_name file.vhd
Here, the following options can be used:
-sc_model entity_name file.vhd
Specifies the entity name and its VHDL source file.
-cpp path_to_the_compiler
Specifies the location of the C compiler. If you omit -cpp path , it is assumed that your
environment uses GNU g++ compiler by default.
-sc_portmap port_mapping_file
Specifies a port mapping file. See Using Port Mapping File.
-Mdir=directory_path
This option works the same as the -Mdir VCS compile-time option. If you are using the
-Mdir option with VCS, you should use the -Mdir option with vlogan to redirect the
vlogan output to the same location that VCS uses.
-verbose
Lists the setup files and other detailed information.
For example, the following command line generates a SystemC wrapper and interface files
for VHDL design fir.vhd:
vhdlan -sc_model fir -fir.vhd

Generating SystemC Wrapper for Verilog Models (Alternative Use
Model)
The
-sc_genif
-sc_genif option skips the check for Verilog source files and directly accesses the
Verilog database. The alternative use model is as follows,
1. Firstly, the Verilog source file(s) are analyzed, which has no connection to SystemC.
vlogan AA.v BB.v CC.v DD.v or vlogan -file \
[<vlogan-options>]
2. Secondly, the SC/HDL interface model is created which does not require any Verilog
source file name but instead uses the -sc_genif option.
vlogan -sc_genif <module_name> [<options>] [<SC-options>]
In case the internal database files are stored in a user-defined directory with the vlogan
-work … option during Step 1, then the same option must be used for Step 2. Similarly,
other vlogan flags such as -xlrm may have to be used consistently between both the
steps. If the specified Verilog module cannot be found in the database, the SC-VDEF-8V
error is reported.
This feature is available with UUM flow only, which requires VCS installation.
• PLI-based interface models are not supported.
You must request for HSOPT or DPI-based interface models. For example,
vlogan -sc_genif <module_name> [-sysc=opt_if | -sysc=dpi_if]
• Options specific to vlogan, such as, the -work option must be used consistently
between steps 1 and 2 as described earlier.
• Generating a SystemC wrapper for VHDL designs is not supported with the -sc_genif
option.

Support for Multiple-Top Topology
VCS supports topologies that comprise of multiple top-level modules, that is, a SystemC
top module (under the function sc_main) and one or more Verilog/VHDL top modules
(svtop1, vhdltop2, and so on).
Under the ‘SystemC-on-top’ part of the design, Verilog and VHDL modules can be
instantiated. However, under the ‘Verilog-on-top’ part of the design, VHDL and Verilog
modules can be present, but SystemC cannot get instantiated in Verilog, as this results in
the SC-VLOG-SC donut which is not supported.
XMR Support
All kinds of XMRs which are currently supported with ‘Verilog-on-top’ and ‘SystemC-on-
top’ are supported with multiple tops. All the TLI features for example, direct access and
TLI adapters are supported.
Debug Support
All the debug features which are currently supported with ‘Verilog-on-top’ and ‘SystemC-
on-top’ are supported in multiple tops also.
Export DPI Calls From SystemC

Support for Multiple-Top Topology
A multiple-top design is elaborated in two stages (similar to SystemC on top design).
During the first stage of elaboration, only SystemC part is present.
Verilog tops do not exist during the first stage. As a result, all the export-DPI calls from
SystemC lead to an undefined symbol during linkage. For TLI direct access, and for
UVMC code, the stubs are automatically generated for this phase. For others, it is required
to call ‘syscan -export_DPI ’

The usage model to simulate a multiple-top design involves the following steps:
1. Wrapper Generation
2. Analysis
3. Elaboration
4. Simulation

For additional information, see “Generating VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules” in VCS
User Guide.

% vhdlan [ vhdlan_options] file1.vhd file2.vhd
% syscan [ syscan_options] file2.cpp file3.cpp
Elaboration
The following flows are supported for this topology:
• Elaboration Flow 1
This flow specifies all the top-level modules, sc_main and SVTOP explicitly during VCS
elaboration.
vlogan testbench1.sv testbench2.sv
// contains modules SVTOP1, SVTOP2

syscan sc_testbench.cpp // contains sc_main

vcs -sysc sc_main SVTOP1 SVTOP2
There can be more options and more calls to vlogan, vhdlan, and syscan.

Support for Multiple-Top Topology
• Elaboration Flow 2
This flow looks like a normal Verilog-top-SC-down flow but makes use of sc_main_register()
sc_main_register()function or SNPS_REGISTER_SC_MAIN macro.
In the SystemC source files, define the
sc_main_register()

name (for example, my_sc_main) and register it.
File: sc_testbench.cpp

{ … }
int dummy = sc_main_register(my_sc_main);

In this flow, the complete 'SystemC on top' part of the hierarchy can be elaborated
using
g++
g++ commands. The usage of syscan commands is not required.

Using OPT Interface-Based Communication Using OPT Interface-Based Communication
(-sysc=opt_if)
This multiple-top topology has the following limitations:
• Multiple top designs with UVMC only work with -sysc=deltasyncoption (default) and
not with -sysc=blocksync option.
• This topology is not supported with partition compile flow.
• For ‘Verilog-on-top’ part of the design, VHDL and Verilog can be present. But, SystemC
cannot be instantiated in Verilog as this results in the SC-VLOG-SC donut which is not
supported currently.
Using OPT Interface-Based Communication Using OPT
Interface-Based Communication (-sysc=opt_if)
This section explains how to use OPT (optimized) interface-based communication to
speed up data transfer between Verilog and SystemC.
Use the
-sysc=opt_if option to select the required interface while generating interface
code for a SystemC module to be instantiated in Verilog, or for a Verilog module to be
instantiated in SystemC.
By default, interaction between Verilog and the SystemC kernel occurs using
PLI
PLI. If you
use
–sysc=dpi_if
-sysc=dpi_if, then wrappers use
DPI
DPI for interaction.
The OPT interface-based communication is recommended to achieve highest simulation
speed. OPT based interface is required for designs with inout ports and the option
-sysc=opt_if is automatically selected in this case.
For example, the following command creates a wrapper for a SystemC module to be
instantiated in Verilog:
% syscan -sysc=opt_if my_sysc.cpp:my_sysc
The following command creates a wrapper for a Verilog module to be instantiated in
SystemC:
% vlogan -sysc=opt_if my_vlog.v -sc_model my_vlog
You can use PLI-, DPI-, and OPT-based interfaces within the same simulator.
That is, you can use one SystemC model using the OPT-based interface and
another SystemC model using the PLI/DPI-based interface, within the same
simulator.

Using Direct Programming Interface-Based Communication (-sysc=dpi_if)
Note the following limitations when using OPT interface-based communication:
• Interfaces containing arrays of ports are not supported.
• Read access to parameters is not allowed from within the constructor of SystemC
modules and objects.
• An instance of a SystemC module in a VHDL configuration cannot be replaced by an
instance of another SystemC module, or an instance of the same SystemC module
with different generic maps in another configuration.
If an instance of a SystemC module is present under more than one VHDL
configuration, it should be bound to the same module under all configurations, and
supply an identical generic map.

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
You can use both PLI- and DPI-based interfaces within the same simulator. That is, you
can use one SystemC model using the DPI-based interface and another SystemC model
using the PLI-based interface, within the same simulator.
The following limitations are observed when using the DPI interface-based
communication:
• The DPI-based interface does not work for models containing inout ports. This is
detected automatically, and a warning message is generated. The PLI-based interface
is used instead.
• You can use the DPI-based interface only with Verilog. It is not possible to generate a
DPI-based interface from a VHDL module.
• You cannot use the DPI-based interface while generating a VHDL interface of a
SystemC module. For example, if you use the following command, a warning is
generated, and the normal interface code (in this case, to vhpi) is created.
% syscan -sysc=dpi_if -vhdl
my_sysc.cpp:my_sysc
Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
This section explains how the SC/HDL interface models allow you to add a Verilog #0 or
non-blocking assignment (NBA) delay individually for each port. This enables you to avoid
race conditions occurring in a mixed SC/HDL design.
Consider the following example, where Verilog is driving a clock signal CLOCK. The clk
clock is assigned to one more clock called clk2 through blocking assignment in the
always block, which plays a key role here.The clk clock is read in the SystemC model
which increments the CNT_S counter on each posedge and sends the counter back
to Verilog where it is compared to the CNT_V Verilog counter, which increments each
posedge of clock clk2. Here, both the counters can be reset with RESET==1.
Verilog Code
module top();
reg CLK, RESET,CLK2;
reg[31:0] CNT_V, CNT_S;
sc_mod sc_inst(CLK,RESET,CNT_S);

always begin
CLK = 1'b0;
forever begin
#(20/2) CLK = 1'b1;
#(20/2) CLK = 1'b0;

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
end
end

always @(CLK)
CLK2 = CLK;
CNT_V = 0;
RESET= 1'b0;
end
always @(posedge CLK2) begin
if (RESET) CNT_V <= 0;
else CNT_V <= CNT_V+1;
end
always @(posedge CLK2) begin
if (CNT_V != CNT_S)
$display("Error:cnt_v=%d cnt_s=%d",CNT_V,CNT_S);
end
initial
$monitor( $time , " monitor :cnt_v=%d cnt_s=%d",CNT_V,CNT_S);

#100 $finish;
end
SystemC Code

SC_MODULE(sc_mod) {
sc_in<bool> CLK, RESET;
sc_out<int> CNT_S;

SC_CTOR(sc_mod)
{
SC_METHOD(P);
sensitive << CLK.pos();
dont_initialize();
CNT_S.initialize(0);
}
void P()
{
CNT_S.write( RESET ? 0 : CNT_S.read()+1 );
}
};
In this case, CNT_V and CNT_S might not always have the same value with OPT-based or
PLI-based interface models because of a race condition. The posedge of the Verilog CLK
signal is pushed to SC, triggers execution of P(), which updates CNT_S and that value
change is pushed back to Verilog without any delay. All these events occur within the
Verilog active queue after the posedge of CLK. The comparison if (CNT_V != CNT_S)
in Verilog also happens in the active queue after the posedge of CLK. The increment

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
of CNT_V, however, happens in the NBA queue which gets executed only after the
active queue is completed. That is, the update of CNT_V comes with a predictable delay
(one NBA) but the update of CNT_S has no such delay, which makes the design non-
deterministic.
Now, you can make the design deterministic by automatically inserting delays of signal
CNT_S on the Verilog side.
You can specify delays (individually for each port) within the portmap file. The format of the
portmap file supports a fifth argument (optional) that specifies the delay.
Example 4 Port Map File
#port width Verilog SystemC delay

clock 1 bit bool none
AAA 2 bit_vector sc_lv NBA
BBB 8 bit_vector sc_bv zero
CCC 4 bit_vector sc_lv
DDD 32 bit_vector sc_int nba
The fifth argument is optional. If it is not specified (or no portmap file at all), then the port
has the same delay as in previous releases.
Following are the valid values for the fifth argument:
• NBA, nba: The value changes are delayed by a Verilog NBA statement: always
@(port_inside) port_outside <= port_inside;
• ZERO, zero: The value changes are delayed by a Verilog #0 statement (inactive queue):
always @(port_inside) port_outside = #0 port_inside;
• NONE, none: No delay at all.
• <empty> / not specified: Same delay as in previous releases.
Any other value triggers a warning and is ignored.
In Example 4, value changes on port clock are propagated without any delay. Value
changes on AAA and DDD ports are propagated with an NBA delay. Value changes on the
BBB port are propagated with a #0 delay. No delay is specified for port CCC, so the port
follows the same rules as previous releases and its value changes are propagated with
either no or an NBA delay. If CCC is driven by SC and the interface model is DPI-based
(syscan -sysc=dpi_if ), then an NBA delay occurs; no delay occurs in all other cases.

Using Port Mapping File
Ports that are not listed in a portmap file (or if no portmap file is specified at all) are
considered the same as if the entry exists, but the delay field is left empty, similar to the
CCC port in the preceding example.
The delays apply only to INPUT and OUTPUT ports. INOUT (bi-directional) ports cannot
have any delay.
Delays can be specified to portmap files for both Verilog-down and SC-down interface
models. Inserting the delays are supported for Unihier, top.v flow, HSOPT, and DPI-based
interface models.
• Adding delays for INOUT (bi-directional) ports is not supported. If a delay argument
other than NONE is specified for an INOUT port, a warning is issued by syscan and
the delay argument is ignored.
• It is not possible to specify delays with command line arguments or environment
variables. The portmap file is the only way to specify delays.
• Adding delays for VHDL wrapper of SC-down models is not supported.
Using Port Mapping File
You can provide an optional port mapping file for the syscan command using the
-port
-port
option, and for vhdlan and vlogan by using
-sc_portmap
-sc_portmapoption. If you specify a port
mapping file, any module port that is not listed in the port mapping file is assigned the
default type mapping.
A SystemC port has a corresponding Verilog or VHDL port in the wrapper for instantiation.
The syscan utility either uses the default method for determining the type of the HDL port
it writes in the wrapper or uses the entry for the port in the port mapping file.
A port mapping file is an ASCII text file. Each line defines a port in the SystemC module,
using the format shown in Example 5 and Example 6. A line beginning with a pound sign
(#) is a comment.
A port definition line begins with a port name, which must be the same name as that of a
port in the HDL module or VHDL entity. Specify the number of bits, the HDL port type, and
the SystemC port type on the same line, separated by white space. You can specify the
port definition lines in any order. You must, however, provide the port definition parameters
within each line in this order: port name, bits, HDL type, and SystemC type.

Using Port Mapping File
The following are the valid Verilog port types, which are case-insensitive:
• bit — specifies a scalar (single bit) Verilog port.
• bit_vector — specifies a vector (multi-bit) unsigned Verilog port (bit-vector is a
valid alternative).
• signed — specifies a Verilog port that is also a reg or a net declared with the signed
keyword and propagates a signed value.
The following are the valid VHDL port types, which are case-insensitive:
• bit
• bitvector
• std_logic
• std_logic_vector
• std_ulogic
• std_ulogic_vector
The following examples showport mapping files:
Example 5 Verilog Port Mapping File
# Port name Bits Verilog type SystemC type
in1 8 signed sc_int
in2 8 bit_vector sc_lv
clock 1 bit sc_clock
out1 8 bit_vector sc_uint
out2 8 bit_vector sc_uint
Example 6 VHDL Port Mapping File
# Port name Bits VHDL type SystemC type
in1 8 std_logic_vector sc_int
in2 8 std_logic_vector sc_lv
clock 1 std_logic sc_clock
out1 8 std_logic_vector sc_uint
out2 8 std_logic_vector sc_uint
SystemC types are restricted to the sc_clock, sc_bv, sc_logic, sc_lv, sc_int,
sc_uint, sc_bigint, and sc_biguint data types.
Native C/C++ types are restricted to the bool, char, uchar, short, ushort, int, uint,
long, longlong,ulong, and ulonglong data types.
SystemC/HDL interface models also support 64-bit floating-point data type called double
in C and real in Verilog and VHDL. For details, see Support for Ports of Floating-Point
Data Types for SC/HDL Interface Models.

VCS writes the portmap file automatically thus making the task of mapping the ports easier
across the languages. When SystemC is instantiated in HDL or vice-versa, you must write
port map file for mapping the data types between the languages. This is a tedious job
when you have many ports.

Modifying the Port Mapping File Manually
To change the default type mapping for a Verilog/VHDL port to another SystemC type, you
can modify the automatically generated port mapping file.
For example, a port of reg type gets mapped to a port of sc_bv type (of same width)
according to the default type mapping. So, you may not get the desired result because the
port of reg is a four valued logic type and sc_bv is a two valued logic type. In such cases,
you can modify the port mapping file to map logicvector to sc_lv of the same width to
get correct results.
For example, the default port mapping file is as follows:
#port width Verilog SystemC
ina 32 bitvector sc_bv
inb 32 bitvector sc_bv
outx 32 bitvector sc_bv
After doing the changes manually, the port mapping file is as follows:
#port width Verilog SystemC
ina 32 bitvector sc_lv
inb 32 bitvector sc_lv
outx 32 bitvector sc_lv
Using Data Type Mapping File
When running a VCS / SystemC simulation, the interface propagates data through the
module ports from one language domain to another. This can require the interface to
translate data from one data type representation to another. This translation is called
mapping, and is controlled by data type mapping files.
The data type mapping mechanism is similar to that used for port mapping, but is more
economical and requires less creation and maintenance effort. Since data type mapping
is independent of the ports, you can create one or more default mappings for a particular
type that is used for all ports, rather than having to create a port map for every port of each
new HDL wrapper model.
Data type mapping files map types, so that ALL ports of that type on ALL instances are
now assigned the specified mapping.
The data type mapping file is named cosim_defaults.map. The interface looks for and
reads the data mapping file in the following places and in the following order:
1. In $VCS_HOME/include/cosim.
2. In your $HOME/.synopsys_ccss directory.
3. In the current directory.

Support for Ports of Floating-Point Data Types for SC/HDL Interface Models
An entry in a later file overrules an entry in an earlier file.
Each entry for a SystemC type has the following:
1. It begins with the keyword Verilog or VHDL.
2. It is followed by the bit width. For vectors, an asterisk (*) is a wildcard to designate
vectors of any bit width not specified elsewhere in the file.
3. The corresponding Verilog or VHDL “type” using keywords that specify if it is scalar,
unsigned vector, or signed port, the same keywords used in the port mapping file.
4. The SystemC or Native C++ type.

Increasing Stack Guard Size
You can use the following VCS runtime option to increase the stack guard size of all SC
threads:
-sysc=stackguardsize:[09]+[K|k|M|m]
If the size is less than 4 KB , then this option has no effect on the stack guard size, and the
default size of 4 KB is used. If the signed_number is greater than 1 MB , then the stack
guard is increased accordingly, but a warning message is generated.
simv -sysc=stackguardsize:100k
This runtime option increases the stack guard size to 100 KB for all the threads including
sc_main.
Guidelines to Diagnose Stack Overrun
Following are the recommended guidelines to diagnose a stack overrun, in case you use
the runtime options mentioned in the following section:
• If you suspect that the simulation crashes, because one or more SC threads overrun
their stacks, then first try to increase the stack to a large value, for example,100 MB .
% simv -sysc=stacksize:100M

Using POSIX Threads or Quickthreads
• If the crash goes away, then there is a chance that a stack overrun has occurred
before. If so, then leave the stack at its previous size (which is too small), but increase
the stack guard size to a large value (for example, 200 MB ).
This increases the chance for the simulation to abort with an SEGV error on the first
time, when a stack overrun occurs. Compile all SystemC source code with debug
information, and start the simulation from a debugger such as gdb or from Verdi/CBug.
syscan -cflags -g file1.cpp file2.cpp

gdb simv
(gdb) run -sysc=stackguardsize:200M
SEGV occurred in file1.cpp line 123
Identify the SC thread that used more memory and increase its stack size by calling sc_stack_size
set_stack_size() in the constructor. For more information on set_stack_size(),
see the SystemC LRM.
Using POSIX Threads or Quickthreads
The SC_THREAD processes can be implemented by pthreads (POSIX threads) or
quickthreads. Switching from one SC_THREAD to another is significantly slower with
pthreads than with quickthreads. However, pthreads have advantages in terms of
debugging support with gdb or Verdi/CBug or tools such as Purify or Valgrind.
If pthreads or quickthreads must be used depends on the platform which you can influence
in some case(s).
The following API allows you to select or check if pthreads are used (if supported on the
platform):
// Wish for either pthreads or quickthreads, return true
// if wish is granted, return false+produce warning if not
// possible.

bool sc_snps::request_to_use_pthreads(bool use_pthreads);

// use pthreads (true) or quickthreads for SC_[C]THREADS

bool sc_snps::use_pthreads();
The request_to_use_pthreads() function must be called before the simulation starts to
run for the first time, for example, before the first call of sc_start(). A good position in
which to place the statement is at the beginning of the simulation from a static initializer
call.
The function returns true if the request was granted. It returns false, if this is not possible
and also a warning message is issued. The reasons may be, wrong platform (for example,
RHEL32), or calling the function too late.

You can debug SystemC simulation errors effectively during elaboration time and runtime.

Debugging SystemC Kernel Errors
VCS provides an effective mechanism to debug your design issues during elaboration and
runtime. You can use the cbug_stop_here() function that is called whenever a SystemC
kernel error occurs. You can use this function to place a breakpoint in this function and

view the stack trace to know the source code that is causing the error. The following
sections describe how you can troubleshoot your elaboration and runtime issues:
• Troubleshooting Elaboration Errors
• Troubleshooting Simulation Errors
• Function cbug_stop_here()
• Limitations
Troubleshooting Elaboration Errors
In SystemC-on-top designs, during elaboration, all SystemC constructors,
end_of_elaboration() methods and other statements (before sc_start) in sc_main
function are executed. It is possible that something goes wrong in these parts of source
code.
Whenever there is a SystemC kernel error during elaboration, VCS generates an
executable file simv.elab.error. This can be used for debugging the elaboration error
with gdb, as you can know which part of your source code is causing the elaboration error.
Consider a scenario where a SC-top design calls wait() within the sc_main() function.
This is not allowed by the SystemC language, so, a SC kernel error occurs. This in turn
breaks the entire elaboration and results in SC-VCS-SYSC-ELAB error. This is illustrated in
the following example.
% vlogan dut.v -sc_model dut
% syscan main.cpp -cflags -g
% vcs -sysc sc_main

………Error: (E519) wait() is only allowed in SC_THREADs and SC_CTHREADs: in
SC_METHODs use next_trigger() instead
In file: sc_wait.cpp:224
Error-[SC-VCS-SYSC-ELAB] SystemC elaboration error
The design could not be fully elaborated due to an early termination of
the SystemC part of the design.
Please read the hints in file simv.elab.error.README or review the
details in the SystemC chapter of the VCS documentation.
The simv is not generated because the elaboration failed. However, an executable
file simv.elab.error gets generated that can be used for debugging and a test file
simv.README is also generated which provides hints on how to debug the failure.

Now, you must debug the design to find the source code line that calls the wait()
function. To debug the issue, perform the following steps:
1. Rename simv.elab.error to simv
mv simv.elab.error simv
2. Set the SYSTEMC_ELAB_ONLY environment variable to 1.
setenv SYSTEMC_ELAB_ONLY 1
3. Start simv from gdb (neither UCLI, CBug, nor Verdi can be used because the
simulation is not yet fully elaborated).

Troubleshooting Simulation Errors
Whenever a SystemC kernel error occurs that terminates the simulation, you can use
the cbug_stop_here() function to debug such an issue. You must stop the simulation
inside the cbug_stop_here() function and look at the stack to find out which source code
statement is triggering the error.
In UCLI flow, perform the following steps to troubleshoot a simulation error:
• Start simv with -ucli -ucli2Proc.
• Attach CBug.
• Enter the cbug on the UCLI prompt to start CBug.
• Enter the stop -in cbug_stop_here command.
• Run simulation until the SC kernel error occurs and simulation stops inside the
cbug_stop_herefunction.
• Use the stack command to find out which statement caused the error.
• Advance the simulation with run to get past this error, in case there are multiple errors.
% ./simv -ucli -ucli2Proc
ucli% cbug

Please wait while CBug is loading symbolic information
done. Thanks for being patient!
ucli% stop -in cbug_stop_here
ucli% run

In Verdi, perform the following steps to troubleshoot a simulation error:
• Attach CBug.
• Enter the stop -in cbug_stop_here command in the Verdi console.

• Click the continue button until the SC kernel error occurs and simulation stops inside
the cbug_stop_here() function.
• Use the stack pane to locate and debug the source code that triggered the SC kernel
error.
• Click continue to get past this error in case there are multiple errors.
Function cbug_stop_here()
Whenever a SystemC kernel error occurs that may terminate the simulation, VCS calls the
cbug_stop_here() function which is useful for debugging. It helps you to find out which
source code statement is triggering the error.
The cbug_stop_here() function has the following two arguments.
• The reason argument explains why the function is called, usually an error that
terminates the simulation shortly.
• The details argument provides additional information in some cases or might
be empty. The callstack provides more information and reveals the statement that
triggered the error in most cases.
This function is only available when SystemC is part of the simulation. It cannot be used,
for example, for a simulation that has Verilog and DPI but no SystemC.
The cbug_stop_here() function stops in the following situations:
• Argument reason=”P: sc_stop() called”:
If the sc_stop() function is called either from your SC source code or the SC kernel,
the simulation ends. Depending on the SystemC version and settings, it might stop
instantly or finish other SystemC and HDL processes also scheduled in the current
delta cycle.
• Argument reason=”Stop: SC_STOP in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and is about to call the SC_STOP action.
• Argument reason="Interrupt: SC_INTERRUPT in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and calls the SC_INTERRUPT action. The simulation
may continue or end depending on other actions from this sc_report.
• Argument reason=”Abort: SC_ABORT in sc_report”:
If sc_report is being processed and calls the SC_ABORT action. The simulation ends
instantly.

• Argument reason=”Throw: sc_report is about to be thrown ”:
If sc_report is being processed and issues an sc_report object. The simulation ends
soon in most cases, however, it may also continue in the following case:
If there is a 'catch' statement in the surrounding source code, then it might take care
of sc_report and the simulation continues. However, if the exception is not caught in
your source code, then SC or VCS kernel catches it and terminates the simulation. If
so, then cbug_stop_here() is called again with reason 'Error from SC kernel '.
• Argument reason=”Error from SC kernel: sc_report was not caught and
terminates simulation ”:
If sc_report was thrown and not caught, the simulation ends. This is typically the
case when SC_REPORT_ERROR was called. Look in argument 'details' for the error
message.
• Argument reason="C++ exception was not caught and terminates
simulation":
If some kind of C++ exception was thrown and not caught in code, the simulation ends.

If the function is reached multiple times during a simulation and you want to stop only

SystemC kernel errors do not call cbug_stop_here().
Diagnosing Quickthread Issues
VCS is equipped with a better mechanism to report VCS runtime crashes caused by
certain problems with quickthreads used during VCS runtime. VCS provides feedback
regarding as to what went wrong and which thread is causing the crash, thereby enabling
you to take specific action to circumvent the issue. For more information on this feature,
see section Guidelines to Diagnose Stack Overrun and section “Diagnosing Quickthread
Issues in SystemC”in VCS User Guide.

Valgrind Usage for SystemC
VCS-SystemC simulation (simv) contains the user C++ code. This code may contain
some bugs leading to crashes or odd behavior. These types of bugs are usually tricky to
analyze, and tools like Valgrind may help quite a lot.
A typical Valgrind command line can look like this:
valgrind --tool=memcheck --num-callers=30 --trace-children=yes ./simv
-simv_arg …
Now the Valgrind usage on a VCS-SystemC simulation is significantly simplified.
The use model is just simv -valgrind with no extra setup.
Valgrind must be available on the machine where simv is executed. When simv
-valgrind is invoked, Valgrind executable is searched automatically from the VG GNU
package.
The simv -valgrind option calls Valgrind as follows:
valgrind --tool=memcheck --num-callers=30
--max-stackframe=600000000 --trace-children=yes
--trace-children-skip=/bin/*,/usr/local/bin/*,/usr/bin/*,/lib64/ld-linux
-x86-64.so.2,/usr/bin//*,$VCS_HOME/* ./simv …
Extra Valgrind options can be passed with the -valgrindopt option. The -valgrindopt
option can be used multiple times.
The following is an example:
void stim::stim_action()
{
m_state++;
if (m_state > 42) m_state = 0;
if (sc_time_stamp() > sc_time(0,SC_NS)) { outx.write(m_state);
// intentional error to be reported by Valgrind
int a;
std::cout << "a = " << a << "\n"; }
}

Input Files Required
To run co-simulation with a Verilog design containing SystemC instances, the following
input files are required:
• SystemC Source Code
◦ You can directly write the entity-under-test source code or generate it with other
tools.
◦ Any other C or C++ code for the design.
• Verilog or VHDL Source Code ( .v, .vhd, .vhdl extensions) including,
◦ Verilog wrapper for your SystemC module (see Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers
for SystemC Modules).
◦ Any other Verilog or VHDL source files for the design.
• An optional port mapping file
If you do not provide this file, the interface uses the default port mapping definition. For
details of the port mapping file, see Using Port Mapping File.

• An optional data type mapping file
If you do not write a data type mapping file, the interface uses the default mapping file
in the VCS installation. For details of the data type mapping files, see Using Data Type
Mapping File.
Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules
The
syscan utility
syscan utility is used to generate the wrapper and interface files for co-simulation.
This utility adds the sysc directory to the csrc directory in the current directory. The
syscan utility writes the wrapper and interface files in the subdirectories in the ./csrc/
sysc directory.
The syntax for the syscan command line is as follows:
%syscan [options] filename[:modulename] [filename[:modulename]]*
Where:
[options] can be any of the following:
-cc <path to compiler>
Displays the path to C compiler.
-cflags "flags"
Passes flags to the C++ compiler.
-cmp
Creates and compiles helpers.
-cpp path_to_the_compiler
Specifies the location of the C++ compiler. If you do not specify this option, VCS uses the
GNU g++ compiler, by default.
See the VCS Release Notes for details on all supported compiler versions.
debug_access+all
Prepares SystemC source files for interactive debugging.
-export_DPI <dpi-function>
Marks the dpi-function for SystemC.
-export_DPI <vlog-file>

Marks all export DPI tasks in the file for SystemC.
-f filename
Specifies a file containing one or more filename[:modulename] entries, as these entries
were on the command line.
-full64
Enables compilation and simulation in 64-bit mode.
-gen_only
Creates helpers but does not compile them (default).
-help|-h
Displays the syntax, options, and examples of the syscan command.
-help -tli
Displays help about TLI.
-idf <idf_file>
Creates transaction level interface helpers from the given interface definition file.
-l
Captures the syscan command and the output of the syscan command into the log file. It
creates a new file if the log does not exist. If a log already exists, which is not created by
the syscan command, it overwrites the existing content. If a log created by syscan already
exists, then the log file is appended with the existing content.
After creating simv using VCS, you may come across some extra content
captured in the syscan log file other than what was captured during a syscan
call. This is because the VCS command internally calls the syscan command.
-Mdir=directory_path
Specifies an alternate directory for csrc.
-o name
The syscan utility uses the specified name instead of the module name as the name of the
model.
Do not enter this option when you have multiple modules on the command line. Doing this,
displays an error condition.
-port port_mapping_file

Specifies a port mapping file. See Using Port Mapping File.
-prec[=<path>]
Enables usage of pre-compiled SystemC header files.
-q
Suppresses all the notes, messages, and warnings (or anything with a lesser severity than
‘ERROR’), appearing in the BMI messages generated by syscan or from tools called by
syscan.
Warnings created by gcc or gmake are not suppressed.
-sysc=<systemc-version>
Uses this SystemC version. Valid versions are: 233, 234 and 301.
-sysc=dpi_if
Uses DPI instead of PLI for value between SystemC and Verilog. Updates through DPI are
generally faster than PLI. The default value is PLI.
-sysc=nodpi_if
Uses PLI instead of DPI for value updates.
Generates optimized interface code.
-sysc=pli_if
Uses PLI interfaces for value updates.
-sysc=snps_vp
Uses this Virtualizer/SNPS_VP SystemC version.
-tli <tli_file>
Creates helpers but does not compile them.
-tli_D <source_file>
Creates direct member access code for all the sc-modules found in the specified source
file, but does not compile them.
-tli_gen_struct <source> -class <class_name> [-o <outputfile>]
Converts a SV class into a C++ struct.

-tlm2
Adds include directives for header files of the TLM 2.0.1 installation (located at
$VCS_HOME/etc/systemc/tlm) to the compiler call. These include directories have
precedence over other include directories specified with syscan -cflags "-I/my/tlm2/
include".
You do not specify the data type mapping file on the command line. For detailed
information, see Using Data Type Mapping File.
-tlm2=<dir>
Same as -tlm2option, but uses TLM installation from <dir>. Note that the definition of the
TLM generic payload class tlm::tlm_generic_payload inside <dir> must be identical
(same binary layout) as the OSCI TLM class shipped with VCS. If the option is used, then
VCS does not automatically add the TLI-3 (libsysctli.a) and VMM-SC (libvmmsc.a) libraries
to the link line.

DWARF Based SystemC Front-End
Debugging With Arbitrary Record Formats (DWARF) is a file format for debugging
information that is commonly used in UNIX-like systems. The SystemC front-end, which is
DWARF based type API is the default interface. This front-end can be used in the creation
of SystemC-down interface models and in TLI direct-access flow. The front-end provides
support for C++11 constructs. It extracts port signature information from the user-compiled
binaries with debug capabilities such as, .o and *.so object files. This is, even if header
and source files are not available. This functionality is not available with Edison Design
Group (EDG) SystemC/C++ front-end.
Extracting the port signature while creating SystemC-down interface models is the only
step that is changed when compared to the SystemC/HDL interface model creation.
This front-end reads DWARF information. This provides a high-level API to access
information about C++ class/struct and other types. The relevant user C++ file is compiled
with the debug information. Then the interface extracts the port signature and other
necessary information. Object code with debug information is a prerequisite with this
interface. However, it is not necessary for Edison Design Group (EDG) SystemC/C++
front-end.
You can create a wrapper for SystemC/HDL interface models from object files (such as, .o
and *.so) that are created by the source files using the g++ call and compiled with the -g
debug switch, even if header and source files are not available with you. The .o and .so
files must be provided.
Following are the examples that illustrate the use model for creating Verilog interface
model for sc_top SystemC module for .o and .so files:
• .o files
g++ -I. -I${PWD}/csrc/sysc/include -I${VCS_HOME}/
include/systemc233 -Iinclude -I${VCS_HOME}/lib -
I${VCS_HOME}/include -I${VCS_HOME}/include/cosim/bf -I/
include -I. -g -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -MMD -m32 -fPIC -c
sc_top.cpp -o sc_top.o
syscan -cpp g++ sc_top.o:sc_top
• .so files

g++ -I. -I${PWD}/csrc/sysc/include -I${VCS_HOME}/
include/systemc233 -Iinclude -I${VCS_HOME}/lib -
I${VCS_HOME}/include -I${VCS_HOME}/include/cosim/bf -I/
include -I. -g -DVCSSYSTEMC=1 -MMD -m32 -fPIC -c
sc_top.cpp -o sc_top.o
g++ -g -fPIC -shared -o sc_top.so sc_top.o -m32
(if you have 64-bit architecture, then use -m64 instead
of -m32)
syscan -cpp g++ sc_top.so:sc_top
Points to Note
• An archive file, *.a, cannot be used as input. This is, because an ar archive file is
not in the ELF format and DWARF requires ELF file type.
• In a regular syscan flow, there is an additional g++ call that compiles the SystemC/ C+
+ header or input source files with debug information. This, then uses this interface to
extract the port signature and other information. The compilation occurs internally. It is
not required to do any changes/modifications.
• If the module name is not specified in the syscan call, specify one or multiple module
names in the syscan call. Use the -sc_module option to generate the corresponding
code.
For example, following is the use model to create interface model for an SC module
called BusModel:
syscan -tli_DA -sc_model BusModel -sc_model BusModel2 -sc_model
BusModel3+BusModel4 BusModel.cpp

syscan -cflags "-g" -tlm2 BusModel.cpp:BusModel
Were, interface models are created for BusModel, BusModel2, BusModel3, and
BusModel4 SystemC modules.
• Use the _SNPS_SCFE_ predefined macro in this front-end to enable or disable SystemC
front-end parsing of certain pieces of code.
SystemC/C++ unused variables might not be visible in GUI because of GCC optimizations.
Compiling Interface Models with acc_user.h and vhpi_user.h
The header file, acc_user.h is provided by VCS and contains many #define macros and
type definitions. Some of these definitions, for example '#define bool int', may conflict
with C++ class definitions in user code. Similarly, header file vhpi_user.h is also provided
by VCS and may also conflict with C++ class definitions in user code.

SystemC/HDL interface models require to make at least some of these definitions visible
to compile the internal interface code. The amount of definitions can be controlled when
syscan is called. Three use models are available as follows:
Use Model 1
Only a minimal subset of definitions from acc_user.hand vhpi_user.h are made visible.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=0
Chances for a clash of those definitions with user C++ classes are minimal. Note that it is
neither possible to include acc_user.h nor vhpi_user.h in the user C++ source code.
Use Model 2
All definitions from acc_user.h (and vhpi_user.h if a VHDL interface is created) are
made visible, except the following macros: ("#define") : bool, true, TRUE, false, FALSE,
global, exfunc, local, null.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=1
The user code can include header files acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h, where the macros
mentioned earlier are #undef'ed in some situations.
The user code must include bf_user.h before including acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h file.
#include "bf_user.h"
#include "acc_user.h"
Use Model 3
All definitions from acc_user.h (and vhpi_user.h if a VHDL interface is created) are
made visible. Only macro "bool" is not visible.
Invoke syscan:
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags
or
syscan A.cpp:A -cflags -DSYSC_ACC_USER=2

The user code can include header files acc_user.h or vhpi_user.h, all
definitions including the macros mentioned above are visible.

Refer to “Adding a Main Routine for Verilog-On-Top Designs” to view the steps
to add a main routine to perform several initialization for the SystemC side.
Bind Limitations
The SystemVerilog “bind” statement does not support binding an SVA construct to a
SystemC instance.
The instantiation of the SystemC module must be a direct instantiation in the Verilog
module similar to instantiating any other Verilog module.

text:
Usage Model
The usage model to simulate a design having a SystemC testbench with SystemC and
Verilog/VHDL instances involves the following steps:
% vlogan [ options] -sc_model sc_module_name file1.v
% vhdlan [ options] -sc_model entity_name file1.vhd
For additional information, see Generating SystemC Wrapper for Verilog Modules.
% vlogan [ vlogan_options] file3.v file2.v
% vhdlan [ vhdlan_options] file3.vhd file2.vhd
% syscan [ syscan_options] file2.cpp file3.cpp
• Elaboration
% vcs -sysc [ compile_options] sc_main
% simv [ runtime_options]
Input Files Required
To run co-simulation with a SystemC design containing Verilog and VHDL modules, the
following input files are required:
• Verilog and VHDL source code ( .v, .vhd, and .vhdl extensions)
◦ Verilog/ VHDL source files necessary for the design.
• SystemC source code including,
◦ A SystemC top-level simulation ( sc_main) that instantiates the interface wrappers
and other SystemC modules.
◦ Any other SystemC source files for the design.
• An optional port mapping file.
If you do not provide this file, the interface uses the default port mapping definition. For
details of the port mapping file, see Using Port Mapping File.

To view the elaboration scheme, see section “Elaboration Scheme”.
Instantiating SystemC Inside VHDL Design
To co-simulate a VHDL design that contains SystemC leaf modules and Verilog/VHDL
modules, you need to create a VHDL wrapper for those SystemC modules which
interact with the VHDL design directly. See Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for
SystemC Modules. You can instantiate SystemC modules in your VHDL design, similar to
instantiating any other HDL design in a VHDL design unit. Other Verilog/VHDL modules
are also included in the design. The ports of the created VHDL wrapper are connected to
signals attached to the ports of the corresponding SystemC modules.
The usage model to simulate a design having a Verilog testbench with SystemC and
Verilog/VHDL instances involves the following steps:
% syscan -vhdl [options] file1.cpp:sc_module_name
See Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules.
% vlogan [ vlogan_options] file1.v file2.v
% vhdlan [ vhdlan_options] file1.vhd file2.vhd
% syscan [ syscan_options] file2.cpp file3.cpp
• Elaboration
% vcs -sysc [ compile_options] top_entity/config
% simv [ runtime_options]

Support for Multiple-Top Topology
You can find the same example with a run script in $VCS_HOME/doc/examples/

% syscan -vhdl fir.cpp:fir
See Generating Verilog/VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules.

• Elaboration
% vcs -sysc testbench
% simv
Support for Multiple-Top Topology
VCS supports topologies that comprise of multiple top-level modules, that is, a SystemC
top module (under the function sc_main) and one or more Verilog/VHDL top modules
(svtop1, vhdltop2, and so on).
Under the ‘SystemC-on-top’ part of the design, Verilog and VHDL modules can be
instantiated. However, under the ‘Verilog-on-top’ part of the design, VHDL and Verilog
modules can be present, but SystemC cannot get instantiated in Verilog, as this results in
the SC-VLOG-SC donut which is not supported.
XMR Support
All kinds of XMRs which are currently supported with ‘Verilog-on-top’ and ‘SystemC-on-
top’ are supported with multiple tops. All the TLI features for example, direct access and
TLI adapters are supported.
Debug Support
All the debug features which are currently supported with ‘Verilog-on-top’ and ‘SystemC-
on-top’ are supported in multiple tops also.

Support for Multiple-Top Topology
A multiple-top design is elaborated in two stages (similar to SystemC on top design).
During the first stage of elaboration, only SystemC part is present.
Verilog tops do not exist during the first stage. As a result, all the export-DPI calls from
SystemC lead to an undefined symbol during linkage. For TLI direct access, and for
UVMC code, the stubs are automatically generated for this phase. For others, it is required
to call ‘syscan -export_DPI ’
Usage Model
The usage model to simulate a multiple-top design involves the following steps:
1. Wrapper Generation
2. Analysis
3. Elaboration
4. Simulation
Wrapper Generation
% syscan [-vhdl] [options] file1.cpp:sc_module_name
For additional information, see “Generating VHDL Wrappers for SystemC Modules” in VCS
User Guide.
Analysis
% vlogan [ vlogan_options] file1.v file2.v
% vhdlan [ vhdlan_options] file1.vhd file2.vhd
% syscan [ syscan_options] file2.cpp file3.cpp
Elaboration
The following flows are supported for this topology:
• Elaboration Flow 1
This flow specifies all the top-level modules, sc_main and SVTOP explicitly during VCS
elaboration.
vlogan testbench1.sv testbench2.sv
// contains modules SVTOP1, SVTOP2

Using OPT Interface-Based Communication Using OPT Interface-Based Communication
(-sysc=opt_if)
This multiple-top topology has the following limitations:
• Multiple top designs with UVMC only work with -sysc=deltasyncoption (default) and
not with -sysc=blocksync option.
• This topology is not supported with partition compile flow.
• For ‘Verilog-on-top’ part of the design, VHDL and Verilog can be present. But, SystemC
cannot be instantiated in Verilog as this results in the SC-VLOG-SC donut which is not
supported currently.
Using OPT Interface-Based Communication Using OPT
Interface-Based Communication (-sysc=opt_if)
This section explains how to use OPT (optimized) interface-based communication to
speed up data transfer between Verilog and SystemC.
Use the
-sysc=opt_if option to select the required interface while generating interface
code for a SystemC module to be instantiated in Verilog, or for a Verilog module to be
instantiated in SystemC.
By default, interaction between Verilog and the SystemC kernel occurs using
PLI
PLI. If you
use
–sysc=dpi_if
-sysc=dpi_if, then wrappers use
DPI
DPI for interaction.
The OPT interface-based communication is recommended to achieve highest simulation
speed. OPT based interface is required for designs with inout ports and the option
-sysc=opt_if is automatically selected in this case.
For example, the following command creates a wrapper for a SystemC module to be
instantiated in Verilog:
% syscan -sysc=opt_if my_sysc.cpp:my_sysc
The following command creates a wrapper for a Verilog module to be instantiated in
SystemC:
% vlogan -sysc=opt_if my_vlog.v -sc_model my_vlog
You can use PLI-, DPI-, and OPT-based interfaces within the same simulator.
That is, you can use one SystemC model using the OPT-based interface and
another SystemC model using the PLI/DPI-based interface, within the same
simulator.

Using Direct Programming Interface-Based Communication (-sysc=dpi_if)
Note the following limitations when using OPT interface-based communication:
• Interfaces containing arrays of ports are not supported.
• Read access to parameters is not allowed from within the constructor of SystemC
modules and objects.
• An instance of a SystemC module in a VHDL configuration cannot be replaced by an
instance of another SystemC module, or an instance of the same SystemC module
with different generic maps in another configuration.
If an instance of a SystemC module is present under more than one VHDL
configuration, it should be bound to the same module under all configurations, and
supply an identical generic map.
Using Direct Programming Interface-Based Communication
(-sysc=dpi_if)
This section explains how to use Direct Programming Interface (
DPI
DPI) based
communication to speedup data transfer between Verilog and SystemC.
Use the
-sysc=dpi_if
-sysc=dpi_if option to select the required interface while generating interface
code for a
SystemC
SystemC module to be instantiated in Verilog, or for a Verilog module to be
instantiated in SystemC.
You can use the
-sysc=nodpi_if
-sysc=nodpi_if option to disable the DPI-based interface
(which is the default behavior).
• The following command creates a wrapper for a SystemC module to be instantiated in
Verilog:
% syscan -sysc=dpi_if my_sysc.cpp:my_sysc
• The following command creates a wrapper for a Verilog module to be instantiated in
SystemC:
% vlogan -sysc=dpi_if my_vlog.v -sc_model \
my_vlog

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
You can use both PLI- and DPI-based interfaces within the same simulator. That is, you
can use one SystemC model using the DPI-based interface and another SystemC model
using the PLI-based interface, within the same simulator.
The following limitations are observed when using the DPI interface-based
communication:
• The DPI-based interface does not work for models containing inout ports. This is
detected automatically, and a warning message is generated. The PLI-based interface
is used instead.
• You can use the DPI-based interface only with Verilog. It is not possible to generate a
DPI-based interface from a VHDL module.
• You cannot use the DPI-based interface while generating a VHDL interface of a
SystemC module. For example, if you use the following command, a warning is
generated, and the normal interface code (in this case, to vhpi) is created.
% syscan -sysc=dpi_if -vhdl
my_sysc.cpp:my_sysc
Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
This section explains how the SC/HDL interface models allow you to add a Verilog #0 or
non-blocking assignment (NBA) delay individually for each port. This enables you to avoid
race conditions occurring in a mixed SC/HDL design.
Consider the following example, where Verilog is driving a clock signal CLOCK. The clk
clock is assigned to one more clock called clk2 through blocking assignment in the
always block, which plays a key role here.The clk clock is read in the SystemC model
which increments the CNT_S counter on each posedge and sends the counter back
to Verilog where it is compared to the CNT_V Verilog counter, which increments each
posedge of clock clk2. Here, both the counters can be reset with RESET==1.
Verilog Code
module top();
reg CLK, RESET,CLK2;
reg[31:0] CNT_V, CNT_S;
sc_mod sc_inst(CLK,RESET,CNT_S);

always begin
CLK = 1'b0;
forever begin
#(20/2) CLK = 1'b1;
#(20/2) CLK = 1'b0;

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
end
end

always @(CLK)
CLK2 = CLK;
CNT_V = 0;
RESET= 1'b0;
end
always @(posedge CLK2) begin
if (RESET) CNT_V <= 0;
else CNT_V <= CNT_V+1;
end
always @(posedge CLK2) begin
if (CNT_V != CNT_S)
$display("Error:cnt_v=%d cnt_s=%d",CNT_V,CNT_S);
end
initial
$monitor( $time , " monitor :cnt_v=%d cnt_s=%d",CNT_V,CNT_S);

#100 $finish;
end
SystemC Code

SC_MODULE(sc_mod) {
sc_in<bool> CLK, RESET;
sc_out<int> CNT_S;

SC_CTOR(sc_mod)
{
SC_METHOD(P);
sensitive << CLK.pos();
dont_initialize();
CNT_S.initialize(0);
}
void P()
{
CNT_S.write( RESET ? 0 : CNT_S.read()+1 );
}
};

SystemC Code

SC_MODULE(sc_mod) {
sc_in<bool> CLK, RESET;
sc_out<int> CNT_S;

SC_CTOR(sc_mod)
{
SC_METHOD(P);
sensitive << CLK.pos();
dont_initialize();
CNT_S.initialize(0);
}
void P()
{
CNT_S.write( RESET ? 0 : CNT_S.read()+1 );
}
};
In this case, CNT_V and CNT_S might not always have the same value with OPT-based or
PLI-based interface models because of a race condition. The posedge of the Verilog CLK
signal is pushed to SC, triggers execution of P(), which updates CNT_S and that value
change is pushed back to Verilog without any delay. All these events occur within the
Verilog active queue after the posedge of CLK. The comparison if (CNT_V != CNT_S)
in Verilog also happens in the active queue after the posedge of CLK. The increment

Adding Delays in SystemC or HDL Interface Models
of CNT_V, however, happens in the NBA queue which gets executed only after the
active queue is completed. That is, the update of CNT_V comes with a predictable delay
(one NBA) but the update of CNT_S has no such delay, which makes the design non-
deterministic.
Now, you can make the design deterministic by automatically inserting delays of signal
CNT_S on the Verilog side.
You can specify delays (individually for each port) within the portmap file. The format of the
portmap file supports a fifth argument (optional) that specifies the delay.
Example 4 Port Map File
#port width Verilog SystemC delay

clock 1 bit bool none
AAA 2 bit_vector sc_lv NBA
BBB 8 bit_vector sc_bv zero
CCC 4 bit_vector sc_lv
DDD 32 bit_vector sc_int nba
The fifth argument is optional. If it is not specified (or no portmap file at all), then the port
has the same delay as in previous releases.
Following are the valid values for the fifth argument:
• NBA, nba: The value changes are delayed by a Verilog NBA statement: always
@(port_inside) port_outside <= port_inside;
• ZERO, zero: The value changes are delayed by a Verilog #0 statement (inactive queue):
always @(port_inside) port_outside = #0 port_inside;
• NONE, none: No delay at all.
• <empty> / not specified: Same delay as in previous releases.
Any other value triggers a warning and is ignored.
In Example 4, value changes on port clock are propagated without any delay. Value
changes on AAA and DDD ports are propagated with an NBA delay. Value changes on the
BBB port are propagated with a #0 delay. No delay is specified for port CCC, so the port
follows the same rules as previous releases and its value changes are propagated with
either no or an NBA delay. If CCC is driven by SC and the interface model is DPI-based
(syscan -sysc=dpi_if ), then an NBA delay occurs; no delay occurs in all other cases.

Using Port Mapping File
Ports that are not listed in a portmap file (or if no portmap file is specified at all) are
considered the same as if the entry exists, but the delay field is left empty, similar to the
CCC port in the preceding example.
The delays apply only to INPUT and OUTPUT ports. INOUT (bi-directional) ports cannot
have any delay.
Delays can be specified to portmap files for both Verilog-down and SC-down interface
models. Inserting the delays are supported for Unihier, top.v flow, HSOPT, and DPI-based
interface models.
• Adding delays for INOUT (bi-directional) ports is not supported. If a delay argument
other than NONE is specified for an INOUT port, a warning is issued by syscan and
the delay argument is ignored.
• It is not possible to specify delays with command line arguments or environment
variables. The portmap file is the only way to specify delays.
• Adding delays for VHDL wrapper of SC-down models is not supported.
Using Port Mapping File
You can provide an optional port mapping file for the syscan command using the
-port
-port
option, and for vhdlan and vlogan by using
-sc_portmap
-sc_portmapoption. If you specify a port
mapping file, any module port that is not listed in the port mapping file is assigned the
default type mapping.
A SystemC port has a corresponding Verilog or VHDL port in the wrapper for instantiation.
The syscan utility either uses the default method for determining the type of the HDL port
it writes in the wrapper or uses the entry for the port in the port mapping file.
A port mapping file is an ASCII text file. Each line defines a port in the SystemC module,
using the format shown in Example 5 and Example 6. A line beginning with a pound sign
(#) is a comment.
A port definition line begins with a port name, which must be the same name as that of a
port in the HDL module or VHDL entity. Specify the number of bits, the HDL port type, and
the SystemC port type on the same line, separated by white space. You can specify the
port definition lines in any order. You must, however, provide the port definition parameters
within each line in this order: port name, bits, HDL type, and SystemC type.

Using Port Mapping File
The following are the valid Verilog port types, which are case-insensitive:
• bit — specifies a scalar (single bit) Verilog port.
• bit_vector — specifies a vector (multi-bit) unsigned Verilog port (bit-vector is a
valid alternative).
• signed — specifies a Verilog port that is also a reg or a net declared with the signed
keyword and propagates a signed value.
The following are the valid VHDL port types, which are case-insensitive:
• bit
• bitvector
• std_logic
• std_logic_vector
• std_ulogic
• std_ulogic_vector
The following examples showport mapping files:
Example 5 Verilog Port Mapping File

Automatic Generation of Portmap File
VCS writes the portmap file automatically thus making the task of mapping the ports easier
across the languages. When SystemC is instantiated in HDL or vice-versa, you must write
port map file for mapping the data types between the languages. This is a tedious job
when you have many ports.

Using Port Mapping File
A default portmap file can be created by using one of the following options along with the
-sysc=gen_portmap option while generating the wrapper:
• -sysc=opt_if
With this option, automatic portmap generation is not supported for "real" and "double"
datatypes.
syscan -sysc=gen_portmap -sysc=-opt_if mymod.cpp:mymod
4-54
RTL Interface Model Feedback
vlogan -sysc=gen_portmap -sysc=-opt_if vmod.v -sc_model
vmod
vhdlan -sysc=gen_portmap -sysc=-opt_if hmod.vhdl -
sc_model hmod
mymod.default_map:
ina 8 bitvector sc_int
clk 1 bit sc_clock
outx 32 bitvector sc_bv
• -sysc=dpi_if
With this option, automatic portmap generation is supported for all the data types
including "real" and "double" datatypes.
A portmap file is not created if you call vlogan/syscan a second time without changing
an input file or removing the csrc directory. For example, a portmap file is not created
by calling the following two commands without interaction to the v_types.v file or
removing the csrc file:
vlogan -sc_model v_types v_types.v -sysc=dpi_if -sverilog

vlogan -sc_model v_types v_types.v -sysc=dpi_if -sverilog
-sysc=gen_portmap
If a portmap file is created, the following message is generated:
Note-[SC-PORTMAP-FILE-WRITTEN] Creating portmap file
Creating portmap file
'$PWD /v_types.portmap'
If the port map file already exists, the -sysc=gen_portmap option overwrites it if the file
has the write permission. It generates the following message if the file does not have the
write permission.
Error-[SC-PORTMAP-ERR]Cannot open portmap file

Using Data Type Mapping File
Modifying the Port Mapping File Manually
To change the default type mapping for a Verilog/VHDL port to another SystemC type, you
can modify the automatically generated port mapping file.
For example, a port of reg type gets mapped to a port of sc_bv type (of same width)
according to the default type mapping. So, you may not get the desired result because the
port of reg is a four valued logic type and sc_bv is a two valued logic type. In such cases,
you can modify the port mapping file to map logicvector to sc_lv of the same width to
get correct results.
For example, the default port mapping file is as follows:
#port width Verilog SystemC
ina 32 bitvector sc_bv
inb 32 bitvector sc_bv
outx 32 bitvector sc_bv
After doing the changes manually, the port mapping file is as follows:
#port width Verilog SystemC
ina 32 bitvector sc_lv
inb 32 bitvector sc_lv
outx 32 bitvector sc_lv
Using Data Type Mapping File
When running a VCS / SystemC simulation, the interface propagates data through the
module ports from one language domain to another. This can require the interface to
translate data from one data type representation to another. This translation is called
mapping, and is controlled by data type mapping files.
The data type mapping mechanism is similar to that used for port mapping, but is more
economical and requires less creation and maintenance effort. Since data type mapping
is independent of the ports, you can create one or more default mappings for a particular
type that is used for all ports, rather than having to create a port map for every port of each
new HDL wrapper model.
Data type mapping files map types, so that ALL ports of that type on ALL instances are
now assigned the specified mapping.
The data type mapping file is named cosim_defaults.map. The interface looks for and
reads the data mapping file in the following places and in the following order:
1. In $VCS_HOME/include/cosim.
2. In your $HOME/.synopsys_ccss directory.
3. In the current directory.

Support for Ports of Floating-Point Data Types for SC/HDL Interface Models
An entry in a later file overrules an entry in an earlier file.
Each entry for a SystemC type has the following:
1. It begins with the keyword Verilog or VHDL.
2. It is followed by the bit width. For vectors, an asterisk (*) is a wildcard to designate
vectors of any bit width not specified elsewhere in the file.
3. The corresponding Verilog or VHDL “type” using keywords that specify if it is scalar,
unsigned vector, or signed port, the same keywords used in the port mapping file.
4. The SystemC or Native C++ type.
Example 7 shows an example of a data type mapping file.

Support for Ports of Floating-Point Data Types for SC/HDL
Interface Models
VCS supports 64-bit floating-point data type called double in C and real in Verilog and
VHDL. This data type is supported for scalar port or array port for SystemC-top and
SystemC-down topology.
SystemC or HDL interface model with double/real ports can be created similar to any
other SystemC/HDL interface models, except that the limitations to use DPI and always
Verilog wrapper have to be considered.
For VHDL-down

For Verilog-down
vlogan <my_file>.v -sc_model <my_module> -sysc=dpi_if \

When creating an SV interface module for a VHDL-down module, the -vhdl
option must not be used. The -verilog option is not required because the
default is Verilog wrapper creation. The -vhdl option must not be used for
interface creation for a SystemC-down/VHDL-top interface module and the
-verilog option is not required.
Extensions to Port Map File
The default port data type mapping defined in the ${VCS_HOME}/include/cosim/
cosim_defaults.map file is as follows:
double (SystemC) -> real (SV,VHDL) and vice versa
All the other type mappings generate a warning message and the default mapping
double-real is used.
However, a user portmap file might be required in case of array of ports that must be
expanded. The user portmap file for the floating point data types must follow the mapping
rule (double/real). If this rule is violated, a warning message is generated, and the
default port type mapping, double/real is used.
Additionally, the
expand
expand functionality is added that is only valid for an array port. If the
expand functionality is specified for a non-array port in the portmap file, this has no effect.
If the expand functionality is specified or enabled for an array port, then the created
wrapper module does not have a single array port but single ports of the same type as of
the array. For an array port of size N, there are N single ports created, and the wrapper
module must be instantiated with the single ports and not with the array port.
The syntax for the newly introduced type mapping entry in a portmap file is as follows:
Without expand keyword
<port_name> 1 real double
With expand keyword

<port_name> 1 real double expand
The following are the limitations with the floating-point data type support:
• Support is added with DPI ( -sysc=dpi_if) models and OPT (-sysc=opt_if) models
and not with PLI model.
• Support is added only for input and output ports, and not for inout ports.
• Support is not added for 32-bit floating-point type float (C) / shortreal (Verilog)
• For SC-down models, only Verilog wrapper is supported, not VHDL wrapper.
• For SC-down models with array ports, expanding the array port is not supported.
• Multidimensional array of ports of floating-point data type are not supported.
